docs.title: Public API and stability policy
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page says what a host may depend on and what may change. It describes the code of the first release, 0.1.0, and of main after it.

All classes live in one Java package, ai.humem.tiervec, and every class that a host needs is public. Some other classes are public only because the classes of the library call each other. This page separates the two groups. The package has the name of the library, and the Maven coordinates are ai.humem:tiervec.

docs.text:
The supported surface is these classes, their public members as listed here, and the behavior that PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md marks exists today.

Public members of the supported classes that are not in the table are for tests and diagnostics. They can change in any release: TieredIndex.setSealHooks, activity, workerAlive, segmentCount, pendingTail, sealRatePerSec and setSealRatePerSec; GraphIndex.seal and GraphIndex.fromSealed, which use the internal type SealedGraph.

The maintenance and diagnostic methods of the standalone indexes (for example IvfIndex.listSkew, FlatIndex.slotsUsed) are supported, but the three standalone indexes are the least settled part of the surface. A change to one of them is listed in the changelog like any other.

docs.title: Internal classes
docs.text:
These classes are public but not supported. They carry the annotation @Internal. A host must not use them. They can change or disappear in any release, with no changelog line.

Class What it is FaultHook A seam for tests that stops a publish after a step Manifest The manifest file of a checkpoint SealedGraph An immutable graph segment, in memory and as a file SegmentFormat The constants and helpers of the segment file (except the three exception classes above) SegmentInfo The facts that a segment file header holds SegmentReader Reads a segment file SegmentWriter Writes a segment file

The test ApiSurfaceTest checks this page against the code: every public top-level class is either in the supported table or marked @Internal, and the two lists here match the annotation. All other classes of the package are package-private.

A module descriptor that exports only the supported classes is not possible while the internal classes share the package with them. Moving them to a separate package would be a later, breaking change.

docs.title: Stability policy for 0.x
docs.text:
The version is 0.MINOR.PATCH until the API is stable (see the plan in issue 61).

  • A breaking change to the supported surface needs a new minor version, and a line in CHANGELOG.md that says what to change.
  • A patch release never makes a breaking change to the supported surface.
  • Breaking means: a supported class or member is removed, renamed or moved; a signature, a return type or a thrown checked exception changes; a record gets a new component (its constructor changes, unless the old constructor stays, as TieredIndex.Config does for its earlier form); or behavior changes against a guarantee that PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md marks exists today.
  • Not breaking: a new class, a new method, a new overload, or a new constant in an enum. An added enum constant is listed in the changelog.
  • A guarantee marked partly or planned in the contract can change in any minor release.
  • The internal classes and the members that are not in the table above can change in any release.
  • The file format has its own version. Read SEGMENT-FORMAT.md for what a reader accepts. A change to the format that an older reader refuses is listed in the changelog.
  • At 1.0 the rule tightens: a breaking change then needs a new major version.

The Javadoc of the supported classes says what each method does, and it is the reference for the details.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

The harness is src/bench/java/ai/humem/tiervec/Bench.java. It builds a TieredIndex from seeded data, compares every answer with an exact scan that it computes itself, and writes one result file that names the machine, the JDK and the commit. It measures one question set: recall and latency of the tier at a size, unfiltered and filtered, and what happens when writers and searchers run at once. Issue #12 (the range of allowed shares where an exact scan beats the graph walk) is the first user.

The vectors are generated by default. Two options replace parts of that: --data reads a real embedding set that a script prepared, and --engine jvector builds and searches the same data with JVector at the same M and efConstruction, so that the two result files can be read line by line (issue #108). Without these two options a run is the run it was before they existed.

Numbers from the harness are directional unless a study states its claim, its arms, its number of runs and its bound before it runs (see "How to read measurements" in ROADMAP.md). One run is one sample. A result file says what the run did on one machine, not what the library does on every machine.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
Maven does not compile the harness, as with src/smoke. Compile it with the library sources, and run it with the Vector API module (the module is optional for the library, but a result without it is a different measurement, and the file records which one ran):

mkdir -p target/bench/classes
find src/main/java src/bench/java -name '*.java' > target/bench/sources.txt
javac -d target/bench/classes --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector @target/bench/sources.txt
java -Xmx14g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -cp target/bench/classes ai.humem.tiervec.Bench \
  --host-label my-laptop --out results/$(date +%F)-my-laptop.txt

With no options this is the 1,000,000-vector run: dimension 768, cosine, k = 10, ef = 100, 200 queries with 5 timed passes, allowed shares 0.5, 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 each with filterScanBelow off and on, then 10 minutes of concurrent writers and searchers. Every option is a --key value pair, and the list with the defaults is the method Bench.defaults(). The ones that matter most:

Option Default Meaning --n, --dim, --k, --ef 1000000, 768, 10, 100 Vectors, dimension, answers per query, beam width of a segment search --seed 42 Seed of the data, the queries and the filter. The same seed gives the same vectors on every JVM (the DATA line has a checksum) --ef-sweep 20,50,200,400 Extra unfiltered cells at these beam widths, a recall curve like the one of GraphTest bench. The recall floors do not apply to them --queries, --reps 200, 5 Distinct queries, and timed passes over them per cell (after one warm-up pass that also measures recall) --shares 0.5,0.1,0.01,0.001 Allowed shares of the filtered cells --scan-below 0,1 filterScanBelow values of the filtered cells. 0 is off (the walk, with its fallback to a scan). 1 scans first at every share --tail-limit, --small-limit, --max-segments, --merge-fan, --build-threads the library defaults The tier configuration. --build-threads 0 keeps the default of TieredIndex.Config --load add add calls TieredIndex.add n times and waits until no seal or merge is due. rebuild makes one rebuildFrom --settle none merge calls mergeNow() after the build, so the searches run on one segment --conc-seconds 600 Length of the concurrent phase. 0 skips it --writers, --searchers 2, 2 Threads of the concurrent phase. There is one more thread that deletes --write-rate, --delete-rate 500, 100 Adds and deletes per second over all threads. 0 for adds is unthrottled --min-recall, --min-scan-recall 0, 0 Recall floors. With 0 the harness reports and does not fail on recall. The CI smoke sets both --host-label the host name The name of the machine in the file. The file is meant to be committed to a public repository, so give a label that says what the machine is and not who owns it --out none The result file. The same lines go to standard output --data none A directory that scripts/prep_real_dataset.py wrote (or the path of a file in it): the vectors, the queries and the exact answers come from the files. See Real data --engine tiervec tiervec, or jvector, the comparison arm. See The JVector arm --jvector-alpha, --jvector-overflow 1.2, 1.2 JVector only: the pruning alpha and the neighbor overflow while building. They are the values of the JVector tutorial, and they have no tier counterpart in the same form (the tier uses alpha 1.0) --quant none none is float32. With the tier, sq8 builds the segment graphs with SQ8 codes (the walk uses the codes, and the ef candidates are scored again in float32). With JVector, int8 builds and walks the graph on int8 vectors, see The JVector arm --targets, --ef-grid none, 33 widths from 10 to 1000 Recall targets such as 0.95,0.99, and the beam widths to try. See Latency at matched recall --disk none An empty or new directory. The index is written there after the searches (the tier: sealNow and checkpoint; JVector: one graph file) and the DISK line gives the file sizes --props 0 The tier only, with --conc-seconds 0: this many new ids and this many reused ids in the checks of the writes

docs.title: Latency at matched recall
docs.text: This compares two indexes at the same recall and not at the same beam width. With --targets, after the SEARCH cells and for each search mode, the harness tries the beam widths of --ef-grid from the smallest until the highest target is reached (MATCH-SWEEP, one pass over the queries each). For each target it times the first width that reaches it and the width before it (MATCH-TIMED: one warm-up pass, then --reps timed passes), and interpolates p50, p99 and the mean linearly in recall between the two (MATCHED). status=floor says that the smallest width of the grid reached the target already, so the latency is the one of that width. status=unreached says that no width of the grid reached it. The queries per second of a MATCHED line are those of one search thread.

docs.title: Checks of the writes
docs.text:
--props N checks what the tier promises to a host and a static comparison does not show. It adds N new vectors and searches for each one at once; then it deletes N ids of the build, searches, adds each id again with another vector and searches for both the new and the old vector; then it seals the tail, waits until the tier is idle and repeats the searches. The run fails when a written vector is not in the answer of the next search, when a deleted id is returned, when an id answers with the score of its old vector, or when the live count is wrong. The PROPS line has these counts, and also how often the written vector was the first hit, which after sealing depends on the graph walk and is not a check.

The exit code is 0 when every check passed, 1 when a check failed (see "Checks" below), and 2 for a wrong option or a wrong combination of options.

Memory, as an estimate that no run has confirmed yet: the harness holds the vectors (n times dimension times 4 bytes, 3.1 GB at the default), the tier holds its own copy of every vector, and a merge builds a new segment while it still holds the old ones. Allow about 10 GB of heap at 1,000,000 vectors of dimension 768 and give the JVM -Xmx14g. The MEMORY lines of a result file give what the run used.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
• Vectors. A Gaussian mixture on the unit sphere: --clusters (100) unit centroids drawn from the seed, and the vector of an id is normalize(centroid + sigma * noise) with --sigma 0.4 (the generator GraphT.Gen of the tests, which GraphTest bench also uses). The cluster of an id and the noise are a function of the seed and the id only, and the Gaussian uses StrictMath, so the data does not depend on the machine.
  • Queries. --queries vectors of the same distribution, with ids that are not in the index (from 2^50 up). They are not inserted.
  • Filter. An id is allowed when a hash of the id and the seed, as a number in [0, 1), is below the share. The allowed sets of the shares are nested (the set of 0.01 is inside the set of 0.1), and the filter does not depend on the vector. A filter that is correlated with the vectors, such as one tenant per cluster, behaves differently and is not measured here.
  • Metric. Cosine. The vectors have unit length, so the exact scan uses the dot product.

docs.title: The exact scan and recall
docs.text:
The harness computes the exact top k of every query with its own scalar dot product, in one pass over the vectors on all available cores. It does not use a kernel of the library, so a wrong kernel cannot hide behind itself. It does that for the unfiltered query and for every share. Recall@k of a query is the share of the exact ids that the answer contains (the truth is the allowed set when the query has a filter). The SEARCH line has the mean over the queries and the minimum. A tie at the boundary of the top k can swap one id, so recall of exactly 1 is not expected from an exact path: the score of an answer is compared with the exact score instead (maxScoreError).

The first pass over the queries in a cell is the warm-up and measures recall. The next --reps passes are timed, one search at a time on one thread, and give p50, p99, p99.9, mean, maximum and operations per second. A cell with scanFirst=true runs the exact scan of the allowed ids in every segment (the plan of DESIGN.md).

docs.title: Real data
docs.text: --data DIR replaces the generated vectors, queries and exact answers with the files of a real embedding set. The set it was written for is the DBpedia entities set with OpenAI embeddings (text-embedding-3-large, 1536 dimensions, 1,000,000 rows, 26 parquet shards), the question of issue #106: does the recall of the tier at 1,000,000 vectors depend on the build parameters as strongly on real embeddings as on the clustered Gaussian data?

docs.title: Prepare the files
docs.text:
The script scripts/prep_real_dataset.py converts the shards once. It declares its two dependencies (numpy and pyarrow) in a header, so uv run installs them, and it is not part of the Maven build:

uv run --python 3.12 scripts/prep_real_dataset.py SHARDS_DIR DATA_DIR --queries 1000

It reads the shards once, holds 1000 rows out as the query set (drawn at random with --seed, 42 by default), and writes the rest as the index. Then it scans the index in blocks of vectors to find the exact top 10 of every query by the cosine, and rescores the best candidates of each query in float64. It never holds the whole set, and one run needs well under 8 GB of memory (a batch of rows while reading, and a block of vectors with a queries x block score matrix while scanning). The 1,000,000-row set gives an index of 999,000 vectors and 1000 queries. --limit N uses only the first N rows, for a smaller index with its own exact answers (100,000 vectors for a comparison with the 100,000 row of issue #106). --column names the column of embeddings (the default is the one of the DBpedia set), and --truth-k the number of exact answers per query (10).

DATA_DIR holds four files. The loader (RealData.java) checks their sizes against the header, and every vector for a non-finite value and for a length other than 1, so a partial or an unnormalised file stops the run before a measurement is made.

File What it holds vectors.f32 count vectors of dim float32 values, little endian, row after row. The id of a vector is its row queries.f32 The held-out queries, the same layout. None of them is a row of vectors.f32 truth.i32 For each query, the truth-k rows of vectors.f32 nearest by the cosine, best first, int32 little endian meta.properties key=value lines: format (1), dim, count, queries, truth-k, normalized (true), and where the data came from. It is written last, and a directory without it is refused

The data is normalised: the script scales every vector to length 1 (in float64, then stores float32), so the dot product is the cosine and the tier (Metric.COSINE) and JVector (the dot product) score the same thing. The header keeps the range of the lengths before scaling in source-norm-min and source-norm-max, so the file says whether the scaling changed anything. A tie at the boundary of the top 10 can swap an id (duplicate rows do this), so a recall of exactly 1 is not expected, as for generated data.

A Euclidean set in the HDF5 layout of ann-benchmarks (such as sift-128-euclidean.hdf5) is converted by scripts/prep_ann_hdf5.py HDF5 DATA_DIR. It keeps the vectors as they are, writes metric=l2, takes the first test vectors as queries with their neighbors from the file, and checks some of them against its own exact scan. Only PacedWrites reads such a set. The other programs score by the cosine and refuse it.

docs.title: What the harness does with the files
docs.text:
• n and dim come from the header. --n or --dim with another value is refused (exit code 2), because the exact answers are for the whole index. --queries is at most the number of queries in the file, and --k at most truth-k.
  • The cells of the unfiltered search use the exact answers of the file. The filtered cells (--shares, on the tier) need the exact answers of each allowed set, and the harness scans for them itself, as for generated data. When it does, it also compares the answers of the file with its own scan of the same queries (the TRUTH-CHECK line) and fails the run if they share fewer than 98 percent of their ids. A run with --shares "" skips the scan, and then the file is the only truth.
  • The concurrent phase is not available (--conc-seconds above 0 is refused, and the default is taken as 0): its writers add vectors from the generator, which would mix generated vectors into a real set.
  • The SEED line says data=file, and the DATASET line has the path and every key of meta.properties. The DATA line has loadSeconds where a generated run has generateSeconds.

Memory, as an estimate that no run has confirmed yet: the harness holds the vectors as float arrays (6.1 GB for 999,000 vectors of dimension 1536), the tier holds its own copy, and a merge builds a new segment while it still holds the old ones. Allow -Xmx24g for the tier at 1,000,000 vectors of dimension 1536. The MEMORY lines say what the run used.

docs.title: The JVector arm
docs.text:
--engine jvector builds one JVector graph over the same vectors, with the --m and --efc of the run, and answers the same queries at the same beam widths (--ef and --ef-sweep; JVector's rerankK is the beam width). With --shares given, it also runs one filtered cell per share, with the allowed ids passed to the JVector search as its Bits. It prints the BUILD, MEMORY and SEARCH lines with the keys of the tier's lines, and a JVECTOR line with the jar, the SIMD provider it selected, and the parameters it ran with. It works with generated data and with --data, and with --targets and --disk.

With --quant int8 every value of the vectors and of a query is multiplied by one factor, 127 / max|x| over the indexed vectors, rounded and clamped to [-127, 127], and the graph is built and walked with byte by byte dot products. The arm has two search modes, and a SEARCH or MATCHED line says which in mode=: int8 ranks the hits by the byte scores, and int8-rerank walks on the byte scores and scores the ef candidates again in float32, as the SQ8 graph of the tier does. The score of an int8 hit is the byte dot product divided by the square of the factor, so maxScoreError there is the error of the conversion. The graph file of --disk holds the int8 vectors inline and not the float32 vectors.

JVector is a dependency of the harness only. It is io.github.jbellis:jvector in the profile bench of pom.xml, version 4.1.0-rc.1 (one multi-release jar for JDK 21 and later, Apache 2.0, see THIRD_PARTY.md), with the scope runtime. A release candidate is an exception to the rule of the newest release (4.0.2): the int8 vectors need the byte-vector support of 4.1.0, and the pin moves to 4.1.0 when it is released. It is not in the library jar and not in the dependency set of a normal build, and the CI job checks that. The arm itself is src/bench/jvector/java/ai/humem/tiervec/JVectorArm.java, apart from src/bench/java so that the compile command above keeps working without JVector. The harness reaches it by reflection, and --engine tiervec does not need the jars.

mvn -B -ntp -Pbench dependency:copy-dependencies -DoutputDirectory=target/bench/lib -DincludeScope=runtime
javac -d target/bench/classes --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -cp 'target/bench/classes:target/bench/lib/*' \
  src/bench/jvector/java/ai/humem/tiervec/JVectorArm.java
java -Xmx24g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -cp 'target/bench/classes:target/bench/lib/*' \
  ai.humem.tiervec.Bench --data DATA_DIR --engine jvector --out results/$(date +%F)-jvector.txt

The first command downloads JVector and its dependencies. The second needs the classes of the harness, so run the compile step of "Run it" before it. On Java 22 and later JVector selects its native SIMD code when the library loads, and the Vector API otherwise. For the comparison with the tier, which uses the Vector API, add -Djvector.vectorization_provider=panama. The JVM line records the arguments, and the JVECTOR line the provider that ran. With --engine jvector, --conc-seconds above 0, --load, --scan-below and --props are refused.

What the two arms share, and what they do not:

Same in both Different Data The vectors, the dimension, the queries, k, the exact answers, recall by the overlap with them With --quant, the quantization: the tier's SQ8 has a minimum and a step per vector, the int8 arm has one factor for the whole set Graph efConstruction, the beam width of the search M of JVector is the maximum degree of a node, and the tier allows 2 M links on its base layer, so equal base degrees need a JVector --m of twice the tier's. JVector prunes with alpha 1.2 and neighbor overflow 1.2 (the tier: alpha 1.0) and adds HNSW-style upper layers, so it is one graph. The tier is segments and an exact tail, and a search visits every segment Build The vectors JVector builds in one parallel pass. The tier adds one by one (--load add, with seals and merges) or builds one segment (--load rebuild). Compare build seconds only between --load rebuild and JVector, with the same --build-threads (JVector's own default is the number of physical cores of the machine, whatever cores the process may use) Search One search thread, the same warm-up pass and timed passes, the query given as a float[] and converted inside the timed call The tier runs the Vector API kernels. JVector runs the provider named in the JVECTOR line Score Unit vectors, so the dot product is the cosine JVector's score is (1 + dot) / 2, and the arm converts it back, so maxScoreError checks the arithmetic and the ids only Memory MEMORY lines after the build (heap and resident memory) The tier copies every vector. With the Vector API provider JVector wraps the arrays of the harness (no second copy of the vectors), and the native provider copies them off the heap. The graphRamBytesMB of the JVECTOR line is JVector's estimate of the graph alone

docs.title: The result file
docs.text:
One run writes one file, results/<date>-<host-label>.txt, in lines of key=value pairs that start with a tag. It is plain text so that grep reads it. Nothing is written twice: a line is final when it is printed, and a file that does not end with BENCH-END is a run that did not finish.

Tag What it holds BENCH-RESULT, RUN The format number, the start time and the host label COMMIT git rev-parse HEAD of the repository at run time, and the number of modified tracked files (0 for a clean tree) SEED The seed and the data model CPU, CPUFLAGS, CPUFREQ, RAM The model of the first allowed core and its flags (a hybrid CPU has cores with different flags, so a run pinned to some cores names those), the cores the process may use, the frequency governor, the memory OS, JDK, JVM, VECTORAPI The operating system, the JDK version and vendor, the JVM arguments, the garbage collectors, and whether the Vector API module and the vector kernels were in use PARAMS, CONFIG Every option, and the tier configuration DATA, TRUTH Time to generate the data (or to load the files, with --data) and to compute the exact answers, a checksum of the first vectors, and the smallest exact answer of each group DATASET, TRUTH-CHECK With --data only: the path and every key of meta.properties, and the overlap of the exact answers of the file with the harness's own scan (when it scanned) JVECTOR With --engine jvector only: the jar, the SIMD provider JVector selected, its parameters, the seconds to convert the vectors and to build the graph, and its estimate of the graph's memory BUILD, BUILD-STATS, BUILD-T Seconds to add and until the tier was settled, inserts per second, the tier statistics (seals, merges, segment sizes, write amplification, back pressure), and a progress line each minute MEMORY Heap in use and resident memory after a garbage collection, and the peak resident memory (also before the build, in a run that uses one of the options of issues #108 and #118) MEMORY-INDEX In the same runs: the bytes the index needs to search. The tier: bytesHeld. JVector: its estimate of the graph and the size of the vectors of the arm SEARCH One cell: kind, share, filterScanBelow, recall, latency percentiles, operations per second, malformed answers, garbage collections during the cell (mode= for the int8 arm) MATCH-SWEEP, MATCH-TIMED, MATCHED With --targets: recall per beam width, the timed widths, and the latency at each target, per search mode DISK, PROPS With --disk: the files and their bytes. With --props: the counts of the checks of the writes CONC, CONC-T, CONC-WINDOW The concurrent phase: adds, deletes and searches per second, search latency overall and per window, every error, a progress line per window CONC-SETTLE, CONC-CHECK, CONC-RECALL The end state: the live count against the expected count, lastError, and recall against an exact scan of the live set BENCH-SUMMARY, BENCH-FAILURE, BENCH-END OK or FAIL, the list of failed checks, and the end marker

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
The run fails (exit code 1) when:

  • an exception reaches the harness or a thread of the concurrent phase;
  • the live count after the build or after the concurrent phase is not the number of vectors that were added and not deleted (a lost or a phantom vector), or lastError() is set;
  • an answer has more than k hits, scores out of order, an id twice, an id outside the data, or an id that the filter does not allow;
  • a search that began after a delete had returned still finds that id (the deleter deletes the ids 0, 1, 2, ... in order, so the searchers know which deletes were done);
  • a recall floor was set (--min-recall, --min-scan-recall) and a cell is below it;
  • with --data, the exact answers of the file and the harness's own scan share fewer than 98 percent of their ids;
  • with --props, one of the checks of the writes fails;
  • with --disk, nothing was written.

docs.title: Rules for a run that is meant to be read
docs.text:
1. Pin the process to cores of one kind and run nothing else beside it. Write down the cores: the file records cpusAllowedList. A laptop on battery, with a turbo that varies, or with its low-power cores, is a directional measurement.
  2. Use a JDK that CI tests (Temurin 21 or 25), name it in the file (JDK), and keep the Vector API module on, unless the run is the scalar one on purpose (-Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true).
  3. A claim needs the runs that ROADMAP.md asks for, each in a fresh JVM, and a bound that was written down before the first run. One run is a description.
  4. Commit the file with its commit SHA inside, in results/, and say in the table row of the README what it covers.
  5. Do not compare files from different machines or different JDK builds as if only the library changed.
  6. Compare the tier and JVector only from two runs on the same machine and the same JDK build, one after the other, on the same cores and with the same --build-threads, and say which JVector SIMD provider ran. The table in The JVector arm says what the two arms do not have in common.

docs.title: Successive merges
docs.text:
MergeGenerations, in src/bench, runs many merges of one tier in a row, to compare the two merge modes of Config.withMergeMode (issue #16). It needs a real data set. It draws rows in an order that depends on the seed only and builds the first --base of them with one rebuildFrom. Each of --generations generations then deletes --delete-pct percent of the rows that are live at its start (at most 25, so that no insert merge falls back to a rebuild because of hidden rows), adds --add-pct percent of the base count from unused rows, seals the tail and calls mergeNow(). The worker never seals or merges by itself, and the writes are the same in both modes.

java -Xms6g -Xmx6g -Xlog:gc:file=gc.log:uptimemillis,level,tags --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -cp target/bench/classes \
  ai.humem.tiervec.MergeGenerations --data DATA_DIR --base 100000 --add-pct 10 --delete-pct 10 --merge-mode insert --queries 1000 --out result.txt

A GEN line per generation has the seconds of the seal and of the merge, the uptime of the JVM around the merge and around the collection forced before and after it (to match the lines of the GC log), the rows the merge built, and recall at --ef against exact search over the live rows. The exact answers are kept up to date with the harness's own scalar dot product, and the TRUTH-CHECK line compares them with a full scan at the end. The SEARCH-FINAL line has p50, p99 and the mean of one search thread after the last generation. The vectors are held outside the heap, so the heap holds the tier, the queries and the exact answers. The run fails when a merge did not take the path of its mode (an insert merge builds the added rows only, a rebuild builds every live row), when a count is wrong, when an answer is malformed or holds a deleted id, or when recall is below --min-recall. The options and their defaults are the method MergeGenerations.defaults().

docs.title: Paced writes
docs.text:
PacedWrites, in src/bench, writes into one tier at a fixed rate while searches run at a fixed rate, to compare merge policies (issue #4). It reads a real data set, cosine or l2, builds the first --base rows with one rebuildFrom, searches the idle index for --idle-seconds, adds the next --inserts rows at --rate per second, waits until no seal or merge is due, searches the idle index again, and then measures the layout that the policy left against exact answers that it computes itself. The policy is set with --max-segments, --merge-fan, --merge-trigger-ratio, and --tail-limit. The tail is not sealed by age. --split-beam both alternates the full and the split beam during the paced searches and measures both at the end. --sealed true builds all base + inserts rows into one graph with no stream, the reference a policy is compared with.

java -Xmx6g --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -cp target/bench/classes ai.humem.tiervec.PacedWrites --data DATA_DIR \
  --rate 400 --max-segments 2 --merge-fan 2 --merge-trigger-ratio 0.1 --out result.txt
Line What it holds STREAM The stream: its seconds and achieved rate, the longest delay of an add, back-pressure waits, seals, merges and merges into the largest segment, and the busy share (the part of the stream during which a seal or a merge ran) BIG, WINDOW The end of every merge into the largest segment while the writer ran, and the write amplification between the first and the last of them: rows built by merges divided by adds. It is NA with fewer than 5 such merges LAT Latency of the paced searches by phase (idle before, stream searches during which no task, a seal, or a merge ran, idle after) and by split beam setting FINAL, SEARCH, MATCHED The layout at the end, recall and latency at --ef, and latency at matched recall (--targets, as in Latency at matched recall). A returned row counts when its exact score is at least the k-th exact score, so a tie counts

The run fails when a count is wrong, the worker failed, an answer is malformed, the tier did not become idle, or recall at --ef is below --min-recall. The options and their defaults are the method PacedWrites.defaults().

docs.title: The cost of polling
docs.text:
PollCost, in src/bench, compares a search that has a SearchContext with the same search without one (issue #11). The context never expires and does what a host does at each poll: it reads a cancel flag and System.nanoTime() against a deadline. One JVM builds a tier of 20,000 vectors of dimension 128 and times 200 queries in three cells: tail (the exact scan of a tail), walk (the graph walk of one segment) and scan (the exact scan of a segment under a filter that passes one id in ten). Each of 40 rounds times both arms, and the arm that goes first alternates. A cell reports the median over the rounds of the time with the context divided by the time without it. The run fails when the two arms answer differently.

The workflow poll-cost.yml runs it in 10 fresh JVMs on JDK 21 and on JDK 25 and prints the median, the smallest and the largest ratio of the JVMs. It starts by hand, and on a pull request that changes the harness or the workflow. It has no speed bar: a study writes its bound down before the run, as ROADMAP.md asks. The cells compare the two paths of the same build. They do not compare it with a build that has no polling code.

docs.title: The cost of a row copy
docs.text:
MappedRows, in src/bench, measures what a memory-mapped reader of the vector section would pay on JDK 21 without preview features, where a distance copies the row from the mapped buffer into a float[] first (issue #27). The library has no mapped reader: the harness holds its own, behind the internal interface SealedVectors, for this measurement only. It writes two segments of random vectors with SQ8 codes (200,000 of dimension 128, and 50,000 of dimension 768), and one JVM then times these cases:

Case What is timed distance-random, distance-in-order one dot product per row, in random order and in row order: on the heap array, on the heap array with a row copy first, and on the mapped file with a row copy first walk-fp32, walk-sq8 a graph search of the same graph with its vectors on the heap and mapped; the SQ8 walk reads fp32 vectors only to rescore its candidates exact-scan the exact scan of every row, on the heap and mapped

Each of 15 rounds times every arm, and the arm that goes first changes from round to round. A ratio is the time of an arm divided by the time on the heap in the same round, and a JVM reports the median over the rounds. The run fails when the mapped section differs from the loaded vectors or when the two graphs answer differently.

The workflow mapped-rows.yml runs 5 fresh JVMs per segment on JDK 21 and on JDK 25 and prints the median, the smallest, and the largest ratio of the JVMs. It starts by hand, and on a pull request that changes the harness or the workflow. It has no speed bar. What a run does not measure: the first read of a file from disk (the file is in the page cache), memory pressure, and more than one thread (the harness shares one scratch array, so a lookup of a scratch array per thread is not in the time). The search cases run with both implementations of SealedVectors loaded in one JVM, as in a tier that holds sealed and loaded segments.

docs.title: The CI smoke
docs.text:
The job bench smoke (JDK 21) and (JDK 25) compiles the harness with the library and runs it at n = 10,000 and dimension 768, with 100 queries, one extra beam width (32), shares 0.1 and 0.01, and 15 seconds of the concurrent phase. It is not a required check, and it runs beside the fast tests. It proves that the harness runs, that its answers agree with its own exact scan, and that the checks above hold on a small tier. It prints timings and has no speed bar: the runner is shared, so a timing is only a ratio inside one run.

The recall floors of the smoke are 0.90 for the unfiltered and the walk cells and 0.99 for the cells that scan first. In the first runs (CI run 43133522549, JDK 21 and 25) recall was 1.0000 unfiltered, 0.997 to 1.0000 for the filtered walk and 1.0000 for every scan-first cell, and a run took 21 to 23 seconds (the job about 30 seconds). The floors leave room for a different structure of the segments from one run to the next, and they are far above what a broken index gives: a tier that returned only its tail would find at most the 20 percent of the data that the tail holds, and the scan-first path is exact apart from a swapped tie at the boundary of the top k. A control step of the job runs the harness with a floor that cannot be met (recall of at least 1.5) and requires exit code 1 and a BENCH-FAILURE line, so the failure path is not a path that never runs.

The same job also runs the two paths of issue #108 on a small data set that it generates (not committed). It writes 5,100 rows of dimension 64 as parquet files in the layout of the DBpedia shards (.github/scripts/make-smoke-parquet.py), converts them with scripts/prep_real_dataset.py (5,000 vectors, 100 held-out queries, vector lengths that the script has to scale), fetches JVector with the profile bench, compiles the arm, and runs the tier and then JVector on the files with --data, with a recall floor of 0.85. It checks that both runs end with status=OK, that they ran the same unfiltered cells and the same vectors (the checksum of the DATA line), that the tier's run compared the exact answers of the file with its own scan, and that the JVECTOR line names the jar. Controls run both paths with a floor that cannot be met and require exit code 1, and they require exit code 2 for --n that does not match the file, for --engine jvector with a concurrent phase, and for --engine jvector without the JVector jars. A last check lists the default runtime dependencies of the library (mvn dependency:list) and fails when JVector is among them.

It also runs MergeGenerations in both merge modes on the same files, and PacedWrites, with its sealed reference, on those files and on a small Euclidean set that it generates (.github/scripts/make-smoke-hdf5.py, converted by scripts/prep_ann_hdf5.py), each with controls.

The options of issue #118 run on the same files: the tier rebuilt in float32 and in SQ8 (with --targets, --disk and --props), and JVector in float32 and in int8. The job requires status=OK, a MATCHED line for the lower target, a non-empty index on disk, no written vector missed by the next search, both search modes of the int8 arm, and exit code 2 for --quant sq8 with JVector. One more int8 run forces the Vector API provider and checks the provider name.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page describes what the code in src/main/java/ai/humem/tiervec does today. It is written from the sources and their Javadoc. Where something is not built yet, it says so.

docs.title: The contract: VecIndex
docs.text:
Every index implements VecIndex, over float[] vectors with a long id and one of three metrics (COSINE, DOT, L2).

  • add, delete and search may be called concurrently from many threads, and a search never throws because of a concurrent write.
  • Read-your-writes: after add(id, v) returns, a search that starts later in any thread can return id. After delete(id) returns, a search that starts later never returns id.
  • Ids are unique: adding an existing id replaces its vector.
  • Hit.score is a similarity and higher is better for every metric (cosine and dot as they are, L2 as the negative squared distance).
  • search(q, k, allow) takes an optional LongPredicate filter and may return fewer than k hits only when fewer than k live vectors qualify.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text: Class What it is FlatIndex Exact or quantized scan over every live vector. No graph. Has serialize and load. GraphIndex Mutable, concurrent HNSW-style graph. seal() turns it into a SealedGraph, fromSealed turns it back. SealedGraph Immutable compact graph. The only mutation is a soft delete through a bitset. Has serialize and load (one segment file, see SEGMENT-FORMAT.md). IvfIndex Standalone inverted-file index with k-means lists and a background retrain. Not a segment type of TieredIndex. TieredIndex The tier: an exact tail in front of sealed graph segments. A tier with an empty tail can be written with checkpoint and read with open. Kernels, VKernels, NKernels, Kern, VKern Distance kernels. Kernels picks vector or scalar code once per JVM or image, for the flat, IVF, and graph kernels. NKernels holds the Vector API kernels for a native image: the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16; its 128-bit forms of the last four are also what an aarch64 JVM uses for them.

docs.title: Flat index
docs.text:
Vectors live in chunks (the first chunks grow from 64 to 4096 slots, then 4096 per chunk), each with a float array, an id array, a live bitmap, and optional quantized codes. A slot is written once and never reused, so a reader never sees a half-written slot. Appends never copy old data.

The read path takes no lock. A writer fills a slot and then sets its live bit with release semantics, which publishes it. Delete clears the bit. Replace writes a new slot, sets it live, and clears the old bit, so a search can briefly see both copies and the result is de-duplicated by id. Writers take one of 64 stripe monitors by id hash. compact() takes an exclusive lock that pauses writers, never searches.

Quantization is chosen per index:

  • NONE: fp32 scan. The result equals brute force, with ties broken by the smaller id.
  • SQ8: symmetric int8 with one scale per vector. No training, so churn cannot make it stale.
  • BINARY: one sign bit per dimension against a per-dimension threshold, frozen after the first calibration set of live vectors. Until then searches are exact.

A quantized search scans the codes, keeps the best rerankFactor * k candidates, rescores them in fp32, and returns the best k. Returned scores are always exact fp32 scores.

docs.title: Graph index
docs.text:
A multi-layer HNSW graph, with the alpha robust prune of DiskANN (Vamana) as a parameter (alpha = 1 is the HNSW neighbor heuristic). Nodes live in fixed-size chunks and never move. Neighbor lists are copy-on-write arrays published with release and acquire VarHandle stores, so readers take no lock and always see a complete list. Writers take a striped monitor of the owning node, one at a time.

  • add publishes the node's own links, then marks it live, then adds the reverse links, then updates the entry point. A node is returnable only when live, and reachable only through published links.
  • delete marks a node deleted at once. Deleted nodes are still traversed. consolidate() repairs the neighbor lists that hold a tombstone, waits (never blocking a reader) until searches that started earlier are done, and then recycles the slots.
  • A replace is a new node plus a tombstone of the old one.
  • Search is a beam search at layer 0 with a greedy descent above. Filtered-out and deleted nodes are traversed but not collected. With a filter, after a visit budget with fewer than k collected, the search falls back to an exact scan over the nodes that pass the filter.
  • filterScanBelow(fraction) (default 0, off) lets a filtered search skip the walk when the allowed share is small. The share is estimated from 256 id slots spread over the index (a fixed number of predicate calls, for filters without a count). When at most fraction of the sampled live slots pass, the search scans the allowed ids exactly, which costs one predicate call per live id and returns the exact top k. Above the threshold the search is unchanged. With the option off, a filtered search spends its whole visit budget before the scan when the allowed share is below about ef divided by the budget, and that wasted walk is most of the cost of a filtered search at a share near 0.01 (see issues 12 and 56).
  • A filter can say how many ids it allows (SizedIdFilter). When that count is at most ef (never below k), the search skips the walk and scans the allowed ids exactly. The count picks the plan only: test decides which ids may be returned, and a count of 0 scans too, so a wrong count never gives a wrong result. A negative count means unknown and changes nothing. The threshold of ef has not been set from a study (issue 12). liveCount() is the number that a host compares its count with.
  • With Params.sq8 the traversal uses int8 codes and the final candidates are rescored in fp32. Construction always uses fp32.

docs.title: IVF index
docs.text:
K-means centroids, one append-only list per centroid, and a search probes the nearest nprobe lists. Until the live count reaches trainAt, every search is an exact scan. Training is lazy. needsRetrain() measures drift, list skew, and growth, and retrain() rebuilds the model off to the side while writers continue (their changes go to a log that is replayed), then swaps the new model in with one volatile write. Searches never wait for a retrain. Deletes are tombstones in the lists, and compact() rewrites a list from its live slots.

IVF has no serialization yet, and it is not used by TieredIndex.

docs.title: The tier
docs.text: TieredIndex is the composition. The vectors in the host's records are the source of truth. The tail, the segments, and the floor map are derived data that can be thrown away and rebuilt (rebuildFrom) from raw vectors, so the code never has to make the derived state durable. rebuildFrom swaps the rebuilt state in the way a merge does: a search that started before the swap keeps the floor entries that its segments need, and they are dropped when that search is done.

docs.title: Exact tail
docs.text: add puts the vector into the active tail, a FlatIndex (fp32 or SQ8), and a raw copy next to it. The raw copy is what a seal and a rebuild read. The vector is visible to the next search in any thread before add returns. delete removes it from the tails and hides every segment copy at once. apply does both for a whole batch (see Batches).

docs.title: Sealed HNSW segments
docs.text:
When the active tail reaches tailLimit vectors, or its first vector is older than tailAgeMs, and the index holds at least smallLimit vectors, one worker thread seals it:

  1. Freeze the tail under the write lock. A new empty tail takes over writes.
  2. Build a GraphIndex from the frozen contents and seal it, outside any lock, while searches and writes continue (searches scan both tails).
  3. Publish the segment with one volatile write of an immutable view that drops the frozen tail.

A vector is always in the frozen tail, in the segment, or in both for an instant, and the dedupe resolves the overlap, so it is never missing. Below smallLimit live vectors no graph is built at all and every search is an exact scan.

docs.title: Atomic swap of the segment list
docs.text: The segment list, the active tail, and the frozen tail live in one immutable view. A seal or a merge builds its result off to the side and publishes a new view with a single volatile write. A search reads the view once and finishes on it, so a search that started before a swap still sees everything it needs and the old segments stay valid for it. To keep that true for hidden copies, each view counts the searches running on it: a search raises the count, reads the view again to check that it is still current, and lowers the count when it is done (one atomic add each way, no lock). A view that a swap replaces while its count is not zero is held until the count reaches zero.

docs.title: Batches
docs.text:
apply(batch) is the write path of a host transaction: the adds, then the deletes, under one hold of the write lock. The tail and the floor map change in place, so a new view cannot make a batch visible at one instant. A batch counter does: it is odd while a batch is applied and even otherwise, and only the writer that holds the lock changes it. A search reads it before it scans and waits while it is odd. After the scan it reads it again, behind an acquire fence. When the value changed, a batch was applied during the scan, the answer may mix the state before the batch with the state after it, and the search runs again on the current view. A search that returns therefore saw no batch in progress from the start of its scan to its end: all of every earlier batch and nothing of any later one. A single add or delete does not touch the counter, because each is atomic by itself.

A search that is in the middle of a scan when a batch opens finishes the scan on the view it holds, which is still valid memory, and discards the answer. A search that starts inside the batch waits for it. A search that starts after the batch sees all of it, because the closing write of the counter comes after every change of the batch.

The query path pays one volatile read before the scan and one fence and one volatile read after it, plus a second scan when a batch overlapped the first. A search that meets a batch waits for the length of the batch (a short spin, then parks of 20 microseconds). A stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search, so the rate of apply calls is the bound.

docs.title: Tombstones and the version floor
docs.text: Versions come from one counter under the write lock. The floor map says "a segment copy of id is valid only when its version is at least floor[id]". Replace and delete raise the floor, but only when a segment or the frozen tail holds a copy of the id, so the map stays small. Searches filter segments through the floor inside the beam, so a deleted or replaced vector never appears and nothing waits for a merge. Each segment counts its hidden copies, and a segment with none is searched with the plain filter. Because the floor is a version and not a flag, an id that the host reuses after a delete is added with a newer version, so the new vector is visible while the old copies stay hidden. checkpoint writes the hidden rows of every segment into the tombstone file, and open rebuilds the floor map from those bits (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md), so a reopened tier hides the same rows.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
A search scans the tails exactly, searches every segment, drops hidden ids, applies the filter in both, and merges by score. Duplicate ids (a replace in flight) are resolved newest source first: active tail, frozen tail, then segments. Freshness.SEALED_ONLY skips the tails. It may lag (a vector added or replaced since the last seal is not in it) but never returns a deleted id, a stale vector, or an id that was never added.

A search can take a SearchContext, one method expired() for a deadline, a cancel flag, or both. The search asks it when it starts, before each tail and each segment, before more than 1024 candidates have been looked at since the last poll (tail scan, rerank, greedy descent, beam, exact scan of a segment), and after each pause while it waits for a batch. When the answer is true the search throws SearchCancelledException and leaves its view like any other search, so a stopped search holds nothing back. A search without a context pays a test for null in those loops.

docs.title: Merge
docs.text:
When the segment count exceeds maxSegments, or one segment is deadFraction hidden, the worker rebuilds the smallest segments (or the dead one) into one segment from their valid vectors only, throttled to mergeRatePerSec inserts per second so the cores that serve queries are not starved, and swaps it in. Floor entries whose stale copies are gone are dropped at the swap, except those that a segment of a held view still needs: a search that started before the swap can still be scanning an old segment, and without the entry its hidden copy would be valid again. The rest is dropped when the searches of the held views are done: the worker looks again every 5 ms while such a cleanup is pending, and awaitIdle, mergeNow, sealNow and checkpoint finish it on the calling thread, so a tier that awaitIdle reports idle has a settled floor map. The optional size-ratio trigger (mergeTriggerRatio) is described with the knobs.

A merge builds one graph from the valid vectors of its inputs. With mergeMode INSERT (off by default), a merge that takes the largest segment and at least one other copies the graph of the largest, deletes its hidden rows from the copy, inserts the valid vectors of the others, and seals it. It rebuilds instead when the hidden share of the largest segment is above deadFraction. The time and the peak memory of the two modes have not been compared, and INSERT becomes the default only if a study meets bounds written before it (#16).

docs.title: Bounds and threads
docs.text:
One worker thread runs one task at a time (a seal or a merge). There is a cap on segments. No allocation proportional to n happens on the query path. Back pressure: when the active tail holds hardTailFactor * max(tailLimit, smallLimit) vectors, add waits for the worker, bounded to 10 s. awaitCapacity(deadline) is the same wait as a pre-check for apply: it waits for room in the tail and returns false at the deadline. apply never waits for the worker and does not look at the limit, so one batch can take the tail above it. add and delete take one write lock for a short time, and apply takes it once for the whole batch. Searches take no lock.

The paragraph above is the standalone tier. A tier made with a HostEnv (new TieredIndex(dim, metric, config, env), and the open overloads that take one) creates no thread, pool, or timer:

What How it runs with a host environment Seals and merges One task at a time on env.executor(), submitted after a write when something is due. A seal by age and a retry need env.schedule, or a call of maintain() from the host's timer. Parallel part of a build buildThreads ranges, claimed by the calling thread and by helper tasks, so an executor with one thread is enough. Permits Every seal, merge, and rebuild asks env.acquireBuild(kind, estimatedPeakBytes) first and closes the permit afterwards. A refused background build waits 50 ms, then twice as long each time, up to 5 s. sealNow, mergeNow, and rebuildFrom throw BuildRefusedException. Memory budget A background merge waits while bytesHeld() plus its estimate is above env.memoryBudgetBytes(). The seal threshold becomes the smaller of tailLimit and about an eighth of the budget in tail rows, at least 64, and the hard tail limit follows. A call of mergeNow asks for a permit only. close Waits up to 30 s for a build that runs. A task that has not started does nothing. Health FAILED while the executor refuses the tasks.

The estimate is arithmetic: for each row, twice the vector (with its SQ8 code) plus 12 times M bytes of links, and 200 bytes. It has not been compared with a measured peak (#13). The budget cannot shrink what the vectors themselves need, and it does not hold add back.

docs.title: Kernels and the scalar twin
docs.text:
Kernels holds the flat-tier distance kernels: float dot and L2, int8 dot, and Hamming. Each has a Vector API version in VKernels and a scalar twin. The choice is made once, when Kernels is initialized: scalar when -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true, scalar when VKernels cannot load (for example without the jdk.incubator.vector module), vector otherwise. Kernels.VECTOR says which one is in use. IvfIndex uses the same kernels.

On a JVM whose preferred float species has fewer than 8 lanes (128 bits: NEON on aarch64), VKernels has no fast form of the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16: its int8 dot is built on 256-bit species, which the JVM cannot map to NEON (138 times slower than the scalar twin in CI, #52), and the other three need 8 float lanes. There Kernels uses the 128-bit forms of NKernels on aarch64 (Kernels.JVM_NARROW) and the scalar twins on any other host (Kernels.JVM_QUANT_SCALAR), and Kernels.quantReason says which and why. If NKernels cannot initialize on an aarch64 JVM, the scalar twins are used, never an exception. The fp32 dot and squared L2 stay in VKernels on every JVM, hamming stays scalar, and a JVM with 8 or more float lanes is unchanged. Kern.dotQ8 follows the same rule, so one run uses one SQ8 dot in the flat and in the graph tier. AVX-512 and SVE are not used.

Inside a GraalVM native image (Kernels.IN_IMAGE) the choice is different. VKernels is more than 10 times slower than scalar code there (a masked tail and a slice-based sum send the whole method through a slow path), so an image uses NKernels for every kernel that has a Vector API form (the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16) when the module is present in the image, and the scalar twins otherwise. NKernels is the textbook form that an image compiles to SIMD code: a static final species, two accumulators, fma, reduceLanes(ADD), a scalar tail, no masks. The species is chosen from os.arch in a static initializer, 128 bits on aarch64 and 256 bits everywhere else (a CPU with AVX-512 runs the 256-bit species), and the image builder must run that initializer, which META-INF/native-image/ai.humem/tiervec/native-image.properties asks for with --initialize-at-build-time=ai.humem.tiervec.NKernels. The initializer catches a missing module and leaves the species null, so an image built without the module still builds and Kernels selects the scalar twins, with the cause in Kernels.scalarReason. The int8, SQ8, and block16 kernels have two forms each in NKernels, one per species, chosen by NKernels.WIDE: the wide form for the 256-bit float species, and the narrow form for the 128-bit one, where the Vector API has no 32-bit byte species, so the byte vector is loaded at 64 or 128 bits and split into parts. Each form is the one that was fastest in an image on both Oracle GraalVM 25 and GraalVM CE 25.0.2, on x86-64 and arm64 Linux (#48). Hamming has no Vector API form and stays scalar. Kernels.JVM_VECTOR and Kernels.NATIVE_VECTOR say which holder is in use. The fixed-order sum of the JVM kernels is not used in an image: a sum in a fixed order is fast only on Oracle GraalVM, so NKernels takes reduceLanes, and its result can differ from the JVM by rounding. To build the image, give the builder --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -H:+VectorAPISupport (GraalVM 25; the properties file does not set them, so a scalar image stays possible).

Kern holds the graph kernels: float dot, squared L2, and the dot of a float query with SQ8 codes (in an image, NKernels.dotF8). Its Vector API versions are in VKern, and its scalar twins are the scalar twins of Kernels. On a JVM VKern sums the lanes in the fixed order of VKernels.hsum, as the flat kernels do, so a graph kernel returns the same bits for the same input in the interpreter, in C1, and in C2, and a segment that is read back is served with the score bits of the graph it was written from (#104). reduceLanes(ADD) was used there before and left the order to the JIT tier. NKernels still uses reduceLanes(ADD), so on an aarch64 JVM the SQ8 distance that steers the graph walk (NKernels.dotF8N, dotF8x4N) can differ in the last bit between two JIT tiers. The score of a returned hit is not affected: with SQ8 it is recomputed in fp32 by VKern. Only a tie of two walk distances within one ulp can change which candidates a search visits. Kern follows Kernels.VECTOR, and Kernels initializes both holder classes inside its try, so one run never mixes the two modes and a failure to load either holder selects the scalar twins for every index. GraphIndex, SealedGraph, and TieredIndex need no incubator class in that case.

A scalar result and a vector result of the same float kernel can differ by rounding. KernDiffTest states the tolerance (1e-5 times the sum of the absolute terms) and compares exactly representable data bit for bit; for NKernels it uses 1e-4 times the sum of the absolute terms plus a floor of 1e-6, on lengths around the lane width and at 100, 128, and 770, for every form of every NKernels kernel, so the 128-bit forms of aarch64 are tested on an x86 host too. NoIncubatorTest starts a JVM without the module and builds and searches a tier in it. The graph, segment, and tier tests also run with the scalar twins, in the surefire execution scalar-twin.

docs.title: Tier configuration
docs.text:
TieredIndex.Config is a record. Config.defaults() gives the defaults below, and with... methods return a changed copy. The constructor rejects tailLimit < 1, smallLimit < 0, maxSegments < 1, mergeFan < 2, hardTailFactor < 2, buildThreads < 1, a negative or infinite mergeTriggerRatio, and a BINARY tail quantizer.

Knob Default What it does tailLimit 2000 Seal when the active tail has this many vectors. tailAgeMs 60000 Also seal when the oldest tail vector is older than this. 0 means never by age. smallLimit 1000 Below this many live vectors no graph is ever built and every search is an exact scan. maxSegments 8 Merge when the segment count exceeds this. mergeFan 4 How many of the smallest segments one merge takes. deadFraction 0.3 Compact (merge) a segment when this share of it is hidden. mergeRatePerSec 50000 Insert rate cap of the merge builder. 0 means unlimited. hardTailFactor 4 Back pressure: writers wait when the active tail holds this factor times max(tailLimit, smallLimit) vectors. tailQuant NONE Tail kernel: NONE scans fp32, SQ8 scans int8 codes and reranks the best 5 times k candidates in fp32. graph GraphIndex.Params.defaults() Segment graph parameters: M 16, efConstruction 200, efSearch 100 (the search beam), alpha 1.0, sq8 false, seed 42. buildThreads max(1, min(4, cpus - 1)) Threads of one seal or merge build. splitBeam false When true and more than one segment is searched, segment s gets the beam max(k, ceil(ef * rows(s) / rows of all searched segments)) instead of the full ef. mergeTriggerRatio 0.0 Size-ratio merge trigger, off at 0. See below.

With mergeTriggerRatio X above 0, the segment with the most live rows is the big one. When the live rows of all the other segments together exceed X times the live rows of the big one, all segments are merged into one. Otherwise, if maxSegments is at least 2 and the count exceeds it, the count rule picks among the small segments only, so the big one is rewritten only by the ratio rule. With maxSegments 1 the count rule includes the big one and a merge happens at every seal. A merge into the big segment rewrites about (1 + X) / X vectors per inserted vector, on top of the small-segment merges.

Other controls on the tier: filterScanBelow(fraction) (default 0, off) is the scan-first threshold of filtered searches, applied per segment (the tails are always scanned exactly), sealNow(), mergeNow() and awaitIdle(timeoutMs) run or wait for the worker, search(q, k, allow, ef) sets the beam per call, and stats() reports seals, merges, segment sizes, floor entries, write amplification, and a log of finished tasks.

docs.title: Configuration as a map
docs.text:
Config.toMap() writes every setting as text, and Config.fromMap reads it back to an equal configuration. The keys are the component names of the table above, with the graph parameters one by one: graph.M, graph.efConstruction, graph.efSearch, graph.alpha, graph.sq8, and graph.seed, plus mergeMode. A key that a map does not have takes the default of the library that reads it, so a host stores the whole result of toMap(). The dimension and the metric belong to the index definition and are not keys.

Moment Method Unknown key Value that cannot be used An index is created Config.fromMap(map) refused, the message names it refused, the message names the key A stored definition is loaded Config.fromStoredMap(map, warning) reported to warning and ignored, so a downgrade opens refused An open index changes reconfigure(changes) refused refused

reconfigure changes graph.efSearch and splitBeam, the search-time knobs. It refuses every other key whose value would change, and makes all changes of a call or none.

Config.fingerprint(dim, metric) returns a canonical text and its SHA-256 over what decides the data of the graphs and their files: the dimension, the metric, the id width, graph.M, graph.efConstruction, graph.alpha, graph.sq8, and the layer 0 layout. The search-time knobs, the tail settings (the tail is not persisted), the seal and merge policy, and graph.seed are not in it. The manifest records the same settings except alpha, and open compares those, so a host that wants a change of alpha to discard the persisted state compares fingerprints itself.
