docs.title: Id epoch and replay
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page specifies how a host numbers the vectors it gives to tiervec, how it tells the library that the numbering changed, and what the host and the library do after a restart. It belongs to the host contract and answers the questions that page leaves open about ids and recovery.

Status: specification, partly built. A piece is built only when it is marked exists today and names the test that shows it; everything else is planned. The tracking issues are #7 (epoch, snapshot rebuild, replay) and #9 (the manifest that stores the epoch). Nothing here is a measurement.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
The library keys every vector by an opaque long id that the host supplies. A host can renumber its ids (for example when it compacts its own storage), can reuse them, and can replay writes after a crash. A persisted segment that does not know which numbering its ids belong to can, after a restart, return the wrong vector for an id, and nobody notices. Without a replay protocol, every host invents its own recovery and gets the edge cases differently wrong.

The library is meant to hold derived data only. The vectors in the host's records are the truth, so every rule below is built to keep that true: whatever the library persisted can be checked against the records, and thrown away when the check fails.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Id: the long that the host passes to add and delete and receives back in Hit.
  • Epoch: a long that names one numbering of ids. The library compares epochs only for equality and never orders them.
  • High-water id: the largest id held by any sealed segment of the persisted state. Every id in the tail is above it. This holds because a seal takes the whole frozen tail, and because add ids increase inside an epoch.
  • Recovered maximum: the highest id the host itself found after its own recovery.
  • Cold: an index with no usable persisted state. It is built from the host's records.

docs.title: Id models
docs.text:
Three models are possible. They differ in what the key is, and so in what the host and the library must do about reuse, ordering, and renumbering.

Stable host id plus epoch (recommended) Host record handle as the key Dense id that a compaction can reissue, with no epoch What the key is A long that the host mints per vector version, never reused inside an epoch, increasing for adds. The host's own record handle, packed into a long. The host's dense ordinal, 0 to n - 1, reissued in rank order when the host compacts. Width Fits a long by construction. A handle can be wider than 64 bits. Packing needs a width limit and an overflow check, and a wider key changes every id array in the segment format. Fits a long. Reuse of a record handle Impossible inside an epoch: a record that reuses its handle gets a new id. Possible. A freed handle can come back for another vector, so a delete and a later add carry the same key. Correct only through the version floor. Not an issue between compactions. Update An add of the new id plus a delete of the old id, in one batch. The floor degenerates to a set of dead ids. An add of the same key replaces the old copy, and the old copy is hidden by a floor raise. As the stable id, between compactions. Delete on disk delete(id). Tombstones on disk are an optimization, because open checks liveness. A floor raise per key. After a reopen the floor must be rebuilt from durable delete events in order, which needs a position in the host's log and an ordered iterator over it. As the stable id. Ordering rule for the library None: ids are unique. The host must send the delete before the add of the same key, and must supply a version per operation, because a counter inside the library reissues versions on replay. None, between compactions. Renumbering Detected: the epoch changes, and persisted state is discarded. A host that moves records changes keys, and nothing detects it. Not detected. Persisted state silently refers to the old numbering, and id 7 may now be another vector. What the library changes An epoch parameter on open and rebuild, and an epoch and a high-water id in the manifest. The in-memory tier is unchanged. A persisted floor, the key packing, and an optional section that carries the host's handle for each row, which can go stale. Nothing, and that is the problem. Residual risk The epoch must survive a crash that falls between the host's renumbering and the library's notice. Reuse across a reopen is closed only by replaying the host's log in order, which is host work. Persisted state is unsafe. Only a memory-only index, rebuilt at every open, is safe. A content fingerprint (live count, next id at the last checkpoint, a hash of the live ids in order) detects a renumbering with high probability and does not prove it.

The recommended model is the first. Reasons, all from the table: no reuse hazard inside an epoch, no width problem, no reconstruction of a floor from events the host may not store, a host mapping that usually exists already (the host finds a record from an id with a table it keeps), and no change to the in-memory tier.

exists today: the in-memory tier works with all three models, because the version floor hides old copies of a reused id (TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, DESIGN.md). Tests for reuse across seal and merge exist: RidReuseTest and the longer RidReuse* tests (#5, STATUS.md). The epoch and the high-water id are stored in the manifest and used at open (see the sections below).

With persistence on, one more rule follows from the high-water id. A host does not add a held id again with a different vector. In memory, the tier would replace it. After a reopen, the replay rule would miss a replaced vector whose id is at or below the high-water id, and the old copy could come back. A new vector version gets a new id. Adding a held id with the same vector is the replay case, and it is allowed.

docs.title: The epoch rule
docs.text:
1. The host passes an epoch to open and to rebuildFrom.
  2. The epoch changes whenever the host reissues or renumbers ids, including a compaction that renumbers, a restore from a backup that renumbers, and an import. It does not change when the host rebuilds an index and keeps its ids.
  3. Inside an epoch, the ids of adds strictly increase in the order the host applies them. Gaps are allowed. An id is not reused inside an epoch, not even after a delete.
  4. The manifest stores the epoch. At open, an epoch that differs from the host's gives a cold index. Persisted state is discarded as a whole, never partly reused.
  5. When the host renumbers while the library is running, it calls onRenumber(newEpoch) at the point where it reissues ids. The library drops its derived state and rebuilds in the new id space.
  6. The host persists the epoch together with its own data, in the same atomic step as the renumbering, so that a crash cannot leave new ids with the old epoch.

Rules 1 to 4 exists today: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) and TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) take the epoch, TieredIndex.checkpoint stores it in the manifest, and an open with another epoch gives a cold index. Tests: EpochReplayTest.rebuildFromTakesTheEpochAndTheSnapshotPosition, EpochReplayTest.theManifestStoresTheEpochAndTheHighWaterId, EpochReplayTest.anEpochMismatchGivesAColdIndex. A manifest of the previous layout (epoch unset, written by a tier that never had an epoch) still opens through open(dir, config), and a host that has an epoch gets a cold index from it (EpochReplayTest.aManifestOfThePreviousLayoutOpensAndGivesAColdIndexWhenTheHostHasAnEpoch, which also opens a manifest with a larger minor version). The manifest layout did not change, because it already had the two fields, so the format version did not change either. Long.MIN_VALUE is not a valid epoch: it is how the manifest says none. Rule 5: rebuildFrom(source, newEpoch) is the call that moves the library into a new numbering, with the tests above, and the host stops applying writes of the old numbering when it renumbers; a method named onRenumber is planned. Rule 6 is the host's side. The library relies on the order of ids and does not check it (planned, #7).

docs.title: The replay protocol
docs.text:
The host replays what the persisted state lacks, and the library reconciles what the host deleted or never made durable. This is the sequence after a restart, with the host's side marked as host.

  1. Host: finish the host's own recovery first, so that its records, its id table, and its recovered maximum are final. The library opens after that.
  2. Host: call open with the index definition, the configuration and its fingerprint, the environment, the record source, and the directory. The record source offers the epoch, every live record, every live record above a given id, a liveness test for one id, and the recovered maximum.
  3. Library: find the newest valid manifest. A damaged or truncated manifest falls back to the previous generation, and when none is usable the library throws CorruptStateException, so that the host calls rebuildFrom.
  4. Library: compare the manifest's fingerprint, dimension, metric, and epoch with the host's. Any mismatch gives a cold index and ends the sequence here.
  5. Library: apply the durable-prefix rule. Every held id above the recovered maximum is dropped (see below).
  6. Library: for every id still held in a segment, ask the record source whether the id is live. A record that is not live marks the row dead. This is a check per held id, not a scan of the host's pages.
  7. Library: ask the record source for every live record above the high-water id, in increasing id order, and append the vectors to the tail. Segments are not touched.
  8. Library: report ready. The host resumes normal traffic: one apply per committed transaction.

If the persisted state is cold, the host calls rebuildFrom over its live records, with its epoch and a snapshot position, and the library reports ready when the build is swapped in.

Rebuild while the host keeps writing: the host passes a snapshot position, which is the highest id covered by the records it hands over. The library builds without blocking apply or search. Adds above the snapshot position that arrive during the build are kept and applied after the swap. Deletes that arrive during the build are kept as well, in arrival order, and applied after the swap, so that a delete of an id that the snapshot contains is not lost. None is lost and none is applied twice. exists today: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long), and the form rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshotPosition). The text above does not say who starts first, the host's snapshot or the library's record of writes. The order that is safe is: the library starts to record the writes it accepts, then asks the host for the snapshot. A write that the host applied before the library started to record, and that the snapshot does not cover, would be lost. So the host takes its snapshot inside the supplier that the library calls, and serializes that with its own calls of apply. At the swap, under one hold of the write lock, the recorded writes are applied to the rebuilt state in arrival order, adds at or below the snapshot position skipped, and recording stops. Tests: EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap (a write from another thread gets through during the build, adds above the position are kept once, deletes of ids of the snapshot are applied, and a late batch at or below the position is not applied again), EpochReplayTest.anAbortedRebuildChangesNothing, EpochReplayStressTest.aRebuildNeverLosesAWriteThatArrivesDuringIt (a host thread writes without a pause while the tier is rebuilt from snapshots), and its long variant in EpochReplayLongTest. The one-argument rebuildFrom(Iterable<IdVector>) is unchanged: it holds the write lock for the whole build and keeps the epoch.

Steps 3 to 8 exists today as TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource), with these differences from the text above. The fingerprint, the dimension, the metric, and the epoch are compared, and any failure to read the directory (damage, a newer format, no manifest) gives a cold index with the cause in openFallbackCause(), where step 3 says the library throws CorruptStateException (open(dir, config), which has no records to build from, does throw it for damage). The replay of step 7 is applied with apply in batches of 1024. Step 8 is the return of open. Tests: EpochReplayTest.theHostReplaysEverythingAboveTheHighWaterId, EpochReplayTest.theLivenessCheckHidesIdsTheHostDeleted (the rows are hidden in memory only, and a liveness check alone writes nothing), EpochReplayTest.idsAboveTheRecoveredMaximumAreDroppedBeforeTheIndexIsReady.

docs.title: The idempotence rule
docs.text:
add of a held id replaces it with the same vector, and delete of an absent id returns false and changes nothing. Re-applying a batch therefore changes nothing visible, on one condition that the host guarantees: inside an epoch, an id always denotes one vector.

Because of this, the host may start a replay at or below the true position. A replay that starts too early is slower, never wrong. This is what lets the high-water id lag, and what makes a crash in the middle of a replay harmless.

exists today for single calls: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete. exists today for whole batches: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.applyingTheSameBatchAgainChangesNothingVisible. exists today across a checkpoint and a reopen: EpochReplayTest.replayingTheSameBatchesAfterAReopenChangesNothing applies the batches of the host again, in order, after open.

docs.title: The durable-prefix rule
docs.text:
A commit can count as final in the host's view and still miss the disk (for example under an asynchronous log flush). A segment that the library persisted earlier can then hold an id that the host forgot and hands to another record after the restart.

Ids increase in the order in which the host applies batches, so the ids the host lost are exactly the ids above its recovered maximum. At open, the library drops every held id above that maximum.

Two consequences follow from the way the library persists state. They are part of the rule.

  • Dead is sticky. A row that an open or an apply has marked dead stays dead in every later generation. A liveness check may kill rows and never revives one. Otherwise, after the host mints a new record with a dropped id, a later open would find that id live again and bring back the old vector.
  • The high-water id is lowered to the recovered maximum when rows are dropped. The host may mint the dropped ids again for new records, and those records must lie above the high-water id, so that a later replay finds them.
  • The drop must be durable before the library reports ready, or the library discards the persisted state and goes cold. The library may always choose cold. The first implementation may do so whenever the rule drops a row.

exists today, without the shortcut: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) drops every held id above recoveredMax(), rebuilds the segments without those rows (mergeNow), and publishes a new generation (checkpoint) before it returns; when that fails the tier goes cold. The high-water id of the new generation is the largest id that the remaining segments hold, which is at most the recovered maximum. Dead is sticky because a dropped row is in no later generation. A row that the liveness check hides stays in the older files only, and every open asks again, which is safe because an id is not reused inside an epoch. The recovered maximum is the highest id that the host found when it recovered, not the highest id it holds when it calls open: a host that minted new records in between passes the older value, and the tier then drops the persisted copies of those ids and replays the new records (a host that passes its current maximum keeps the old vectors under the re-minted ids, which is a host error that the library cannot see). Tests: EpochReplayTest.idsAboveTheRecoveredMaximumAreDroppedBeforeTheIndexIsReady (the host forgets 40 adds and mints the same ids again for other vectors: this open and a later one return the new vectors only, and a reader that knows nothing about the host finds none of the lost rows), EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop, and its long variant in EpochReplayLongTest.

The rule covers adds. It does not say what happens to a delete that the library persisted (a compacted segment) and the host then forgot: the record is live again in the host, with an id at or below the recovered maximum, and no segment holds it any more, so nothing replays it. The tests keep to the safer reading: the host makes its deletes durable before it lets the library checkpoint (FakeHost.flushDeletes). The contract needs a sentence on this from the host's side, or a decision that the library refuses to persist a delete that the host has not confirmed.

docs.title: What a crash leaves, at each point
docs.text:
A process kill is assumed. No claim is made about power loss until a test says otherwise (#17).

The crash falls What is durable What the next open does In the host, before its commit is durable Nothing of this batch, in the host or in the library. Nothing to do. The library never saw the batch, because the host applies only when changes stand. After the host's commit is durable and before apply ran The host's records. Step 7 of the replay: the live records above the high-water id come back into the tail. After apply, before any seal The host's records. The tail was in memory only. As above. During a seal or merge, before the new manifest is durable The previous generation, plus an orphan segment file. The previous generation opens. The orphan is deleted. The records above its high-water id are replayed. After a new manifest is durable, and the host lost the commit that its segment holds A segment that holds ids the host no longer has. The durable-prefix rule drops the ids above the recovered maximum. After a delete was applied in memory and before a manifest recorded it The host's records without the record. Step 6: the liveness check marks the row dead. During a rebuild The previous persisted state. A rebuild replaces state only at the swap and publishes a new manifest after it. The previous state opens, or the host rebuilds again. After the host renumbered, before the library heard of it The host's new numbering and its epoch, if it persisted them with the renumbering (rule 6). Old segments with the old epoch. The epoch differs, so the index is cold and the host rebuilds. In the middle of a replay Nothing new. A replay changes nothing durable until the next publish. The same replay again. It is idempotent. A segment or manifest is damaged Whatever damage the file has. CorruptStateException, and the host calls rebuildFrom. A second failure is a host error.

exists today for a process kill: EpochReplayTest.aCrashAtEveryStepOfAPublishLeavesAnIndexThatMatchesTheHost runs the fault hook after each of the six publish steps, and EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop crashes the host and the tier at random points (sometimes in the middle of a publish) and checks after every reopen that the tier holds exactly the host's live records, each with the host's vector. The row for a crash in the middle of a replay has no test of its own: a replay changes nothing durable, and applying a batch again is tested. No claim is made about power loss (#17).

docs.title: Open questions for a host
docs.text:
A host answers these before it relies on the protocol. A different answer changes a rule above.

  1. Can the host persist an epoch atomically with any renumbering of its ids? If it cannot, the library has only the content fingerprint, which detects a renumbering with high probability and does not prove it, and the host must accept a rebuild after every compaction, or a memory-only index.
  2. Does the host report every path that reissues ids? Compaction is the obvious one. A restore from a backup, an import, a rebuild of the host's own tables, and the installation of a replica's snapshot are others.
  3. Are ids minted in the order in which the host applies batches, even with concurrent transactions? The rule needs a strictly increasing order, so the host serializes apply per index and mints in that order, or it mints under a lock that gives the same order.
  4. Can the host list its live records above a given id without scanning everything, and test one id for liveness in constant time? The cost of step 6 and step 7 is the cost of these two calls.
  5. Can the host tell the highest id it recovered after a crash? Under which flush modes can a commit that it counted as final be lost?
  6. Does the host call apply only when changes stand? If it must apply earlier, it must undo an add with a delete and a delete with an add of the vector, and the persisted state then may contain ids of transactions that did not stand, which only the durable-prefix rule covers.
  7. When does the host open the index relative to its own recovery? The library needs final records.
  8. What does a replica, a restored copy, or a copy from a backup contain? The library's files may be absent or older than the records. Absent files give a cold index.
  9. How much memory does the staging of a long transaction hold until it applies? The library does not bound that.

docs.title: Host contract
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page states what a database (the host) must provide to embed tiervec, and what tiervec guarantees in return. It is written for an engine developer who reviews the contract before writing an adapter. The word provider appears in the file name: tiervec is the provider of a vector index, and the host is the database that calls it.

The library is experimental and is not wired into any database yet. Most lines below describe where the library is going, not where it is. Every line carries a mark, so a reader can tell a promise from a plan. Nothing here is a measurement: measurements will be published with the harness.

Two companion pages go deeper where a topic is large: ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md for ids, epochs, and recovery after a crash, and DESIGN.md for what the code does today.

docs.title: Purpose and non-goals
docs.text:
A host that embeds an index has to know what is atomic, who sees a write and when, which calls may block, which threads the library creates, and what happens after a crash. This page is the one place where those answers live, so a reviewer does not have to read the code.

The contract is written in host terms and names no particular database. The host-side interfaces use only long, float[], Map<String, String>, java.util.concurrent.Executor, and java.util.function types, so the library needs no dependency on any database.

Non-goals:

  • Transactions. The library has no rollback and no notion of uncommitted rows. They stay on the host side.
  • Record storage. The host's records are the source of truth. Everything the library keeps is derived and can be rebuilt from them.
  • A query language, a server, or a network. The host parses its own queries and hands the library vectors and allowed-id sets.
  • Ordering across several indexes.

docs.title: Reading the marks
docs.text:
• exists today: built on the main branch at the time of writing, and checked by a test that the status table at the end names. The class and method are named.
  • partly: a form of the guarantee exists, or it is built and no dedicated test checks it. The line says what is missing.
  • planned: not built. The issue number is the tracking issue, and the acceptance test in that issue is the bar.

Names of planned interfaces and methods are descriptive, not final. The Java package is ai.humem.tiervec.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
What the host must provide:

  1. Ids: an opaque long per vector version, minted by the host, unique inside an epoch, and strictly increasing for adds inside an epoch. The epoch changes whenever the host renumbers.
  2. Apply order: one batch per committed transaction per index, applied only when the transaction's changes stand, serialized per index.
  3. Records: a way to read every live record, to ask whether an id is live, and to learn the highest id the host itself recovered after a crash.
  4. Resources: an executor, a build permit, and a memory budget, so the library creates no thread of its own, and a capacity check before each batch.
  5. Transactions: the overlay of uncommitted rows, the mapping from ids to the host's records, and the translation of the host's filters into an allowed-id predicate.

What tiervec guarantees:

  1. A batch is visible as a unit. After apply returns, a search that starts later sees the adds and not the deletes, and applying the same batch again changes nothing visible.
  2. A search returns at most k hits, best first, with no duplicate id and no id deleted before the search started. The allowed-id predicate is applied inside the search. The query path takes no lock and creates no thread, but a search waits while a batch is being applied (see apply(batch)).
  3. A search stops at a deadline or a cancel flag that the host supplies.
  4. After a reopen, the persisted state is either reconciled with the host's records or discarded in favor of a rebuild. It never returns a vector for an id that now means a different vector.
  5. Errors are unchecked and classified, and a contract version and a capability set tell the host what exists.

docs.title: Roles and host interfaces
docs.text:
The library defines three small interfaces for itself. A separate adapter, outside the library core, implements them on top of the host's own classes. No host class appears in the library's API.

Interface What the host supplies Status Environment An executor for every seal, merge, and build task. A build permit: ask with a kind and an estimate of peak bytes, receive a permit or a refusal. A memory budget in bytes, read at each decision. A metric sink with counters and gauges. exists today: HostEnv, taken by the TieredIndex constructor and the open overloads, tested by HostEnvTest Record source The host's epoch. Every live record. Every live record with an id above a given id. A liveness test for one id. The highest id the host recovered after its own crash. exists today: RecordSource, used by TieredIndex.open, tested by EpochReplayTest with a fake host Search context One method, expired(), that says whether the search has to stop (a deadline, a cancel flag, or both), polled by the library during a search. exists today: SearchContext, taken by the TieredIndex.search overloads, tested by SearchContextTest

The library has all three. A tier made without an environment runs one worker thread and, during a seal or a merge, a few build threads (Config.buildThreads).

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
Each row names who does what. "Host" is the adapter on the host side, "library" is tiervec.

Operation Host does Library guarantees Status add(id, vector) and delete(id), single calls Calls them with the rules of the identity section. Each call is atomic and visible to the next search in any thread. add of a held id replaces its vector. delete returns true when the id existed. exists today: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, VecIndex apply(batch) Calls it with an ordered list of adds and deletes, once per committed transaction per index, serialized per index, with add ids strictly increasing inside the epoch. The whole batch becomes visible together: adds are applied before deletes, under one hold of the write lock, and a search sees all of the batch or none of it. Re-applying a batch changes nothing visible. A search that overlaps a batch waits for it or runs again, so a batch can delay a search by its own length. exists today: TieredIndex.apply. Tests: ApplyBatchTest (visibility, a search held across a batch, re-apply), ApplyStressTest (slow: updater and searcher threads) awaitCapacity(deadline) Calls it before apply, outside any lock of its own. Waits for room in the tail or returns false. apply itself never sleeps on the library's maintenance. The behavior at the hard tail limit is defined and tested: apply does not look at the limit, and one batch may take the tail above it. exists today: TieredIndex.awaitCapacity, with the deadline on the System.nanoTime() clock. Test: ApplyBatchTest.behaviorAtTheHardTailLimit. The single call TieredIndex.add keeps its own wait of up to 10 s at the hard limit search(query, k, allowed, context) Passes the query, k, an allowed-id predicate (optionally with a size hint), and a search context. At most k hits, best first, no duplicate id, no deleted id, fewer than k only when fewer qualify. A search stops when the context says so. exists today: TieredIndex.search, three overloads without a context and three with one (SearchContextTest). Size hint: SizedIdFilter (SizedIdFilterTest) open(config, fingerprint, environment, record source, directory) Passes the index definition (dimension, metric), the configuration, its fingerprint, the interfaces above, and a directory that only this node uses (or none, for memory only). Returns ready or cold. A mismatch of fingerprint, dimension, metric, or epoch discards persisted state and returns cold, never a wrong answer. partly: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) checks the epoch, drops ids above the recovered maximum, hides ids that are not live, and replays the live records above the high-water id (EpochReplayTest). An overload takes a HostEnv too. It takes no fingerprint: the host compares Config.fingerprint with the one it stored before it calls open, and open itself compares the dimension, the metric, M, efConstruction, and SQ8. It needs a directory, and a cold index is built on the calling thread (#13) awaitReady(deadline) Calls it before the first search of a cold index, and from its own warm-up hook. Builds from the record source on the host executor under a host permit, never on the caller's query thread unless the caller asks for that. planned (#9, #13) rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshot position) Calls it for a first build, a rebuild, the fallback after corruption, and after a renumbering. Replaces all derived state without blocking apply or search. Adds and deletes that arrive during the build are kept and applied after the swap. Streams the records instead of copying them first. exists today for the epoch, the snapshot position, and the catch-up: TieredIndex.rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) and rebuildFrom(records, epoch, snapshotPosition), tested by EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap and EpochReplayStressTest.aRebuildNeverLosesAWriteThatArrivesDuringIt. partly for the rest: the build copies all records into a map first instead of streaming them and runs on the calling thread (#13), and the swap holds the write lock while the recorded writes are applied. The form rebuildFrom(Iterable) still holds the write lock for the whole build flush() Calls it where the host flushes its own indexes. Writes the manifest and any dirty state, returns when durable, idempotent. planned (#9) close() Calls it when the host closes the index. Stops accepting work, waits for or cancels the tasks it submitted, releases files, idempotent, never creates a thread. exists today: TieredIndex.close() stops the worker thread, or with a HostEnv waits (up to 30 s) for a build that runs while a task that has not started does nothing, and a second call is harmless. Later calls that read or change vectors or files throw ClosedException, and a search that was running finishes or throws it (HostContractTest, HostEnvTest) drop() and clear() Calls drop when the index is deleted and clear when its data is truncated. Drops derived state and rebuilds in the new id space. partly: rebuildFrom(source, newEpoch) does it. onRenumber as a named call is not built, and the host stops applying writes of the old numbering when it renumbers metrics Reads it into its own statistics. A map of counters and gauges, plus an optional push sink. exists today: TieredIndex.metrics and TieredIndex.bindMetrics, and TieredIndex.stats() as a record (HostContractTest) contractVersion(), capabilities(), health() Checks them at creation and when index metadata changes. A major and a minor number, a capability set, and a health state. exists today: TieredIndex.contractVersion, capabilities, health (HostContractTest) Suspend and resume of background maintenance Calls it around a bulk load. No seal or merge starts while suspended. apply still works. planned, no issue filed yet

docs.title: Identity and the epoch
docs.text:
The library keys every vector by an opaque long id that the host supplies. The id is not a record id of the host: a record id can be reused after a delete, can be wider than 64 bits, and can change when the host moves a record. An id inside an epoch cannot be reused.

  • The host mints ids. They are unique inside an epoch, and the ids of adds strictly increase inside an epoch. Gaps are allowed. exists today: ids are plain long values in VecIndex.add, Hit, and TieredIndex.IdVector. A check of the ordering rule is planned (#7): the library relies on it for the high-water id and does not verify it.
  • An update is a new id plus a delete of the old id, sent in one batch. The library needs nothing special for it: two ids, and the delete hides the old copy. exists today as one batch (TieredIndex.apply) and as two calls.
  • The epoch names one numbering of ids. The host passes it to open and rebuildFrom. The manifest stores it. A different epoch means persisted state is discarded and the index starts cold. exists today: EpochReplayTest.anEpochMismatchGivesAColdIndex and EpochReplayTest.theManifestStoresTheEpochAndTheHighWaterId.
  • A host that reuses ids anyway (a record id used directly as the key) is served in memory by the version floor: an id added after a delete is visible, and the old copies stay hidden. partly: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete, and the floor described in DESIGN.md are built, and the tests cover delete followed by add of the same id across seal and merge (RidReuseTest and the longer RidReuse* tests, #5, STATUS.md). Persisting such a tier is not covered by this contract.

The id models, their consequences, and the open questions are in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md.

docs.title: Mutation, replay, and ordering
docs.text:
• Idempotence. add of a held id replaces it with the same vector, and delete of an absent id returns false and changes nothing. A host may therefore replay a batch after a crash, and replaying one that was already applied changes nothing visible. exists today for single calls: TieredIndex.add, TieredIndex.delete. exists today for whole batches: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.applyingTheSameBatchAgainChangesNothingVisible.
  • Order. Inside a batch, adds are applied before deletes. Across batches, the host serializes calls per index. The library needs no remove-before-add rule, because ids are unique. exists today: TieredIndex.apply, tested by ApplyBatchTest.theWholeBatchIsVisibleAfterApplyReturns (an id that one batch adds and deletes ends deleted).
  • Apply at commit, or apply after validation. The recommended host behavior is to stage a transaction's changes and call apply only when the changes stand. The library then never sees an id of a rolled-back transaction and needs no retract operation. The reason is that a sealed segment is immutable and can be made durable on its own schedule: a row applied too early and then rolled back can be sealed before the rollback runs. The floor hides it from results, but the segment still holds a row for an id the host has forgotten, and the host may hand that id to another record after a restart. The library has no transaction notion, so nothing in it contradicts deferred apply. exists today on the library side, as a property of the code with nothing to test. Staging is the adapter's job.
  • A host that cannot defer can undo an add with delete and undo a delete by adding the vector again. The version floor makes that correct in memory. The library has no retract operation. The capability set says which style a library version supports: Capability.DEFERRED_APPLY, and there is no capability for a retract. exists today: TieredIndex.capabilities.
  • Replay after a reopen: the host replays every live record above the manifest's high-water id, and the library checks liveness of every id it holds. Specified in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. exists today: TieredIndex.open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource), tested by EpochReplayTest.theHostReplaysEverythingAboveTheHighWaterId and EpochReplayTest.theLivenessCheckHidesIdsTheHostDeleted.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
• Arguments: a query vector, k, an allowed-id predicate (or none), and a context. An optional effort knob sets the beam width of the segment search. A non-positive k returns an empty result. exists today: TieredIndex.search(float[], int, LongPredicate), search(..., Freshness), search(..., int ef), each also with a SearchContext as the last argument.
  • Result: at most k hits, best first, each Hit(id, score), no duplicate ids. Fewer than k only when fewer live vectors qualify. exists today: VecIndex.search, Hit.
  • Score: higher is better for every metric. Cosine and dot are returned as they are, L2 as the negative squared distance. A host whose engine uses a distance where lower is better converts, and checks the conversion with a parity test on the same data. exists today: Hit. A public scorer for a single pair of vectors, which a host needs to score its own uncommitted rows with the same arithmetic, is planned, no issue filed yet.
  • Exactness flag: SearchResult.exact tells the host that no segment was searched and the tail scan was exact. exists today: TieredIndex.search(..., Freshness).
  • Allowed-id predicate. The host supplies a LongPredicate. It must be cheap, side-effect free, safe to call more than once for the same id, and it must not call back into the index. The library applies it inside the segment search and the tail scan, so the top k of the qualifying set is correct, and a graph walk with few qualifying ids falls back to an exact scan after a visit budget. exists today: the predicate parameter of TieredIndex.search. Correctness of filtered search is checked by unit tests. How it behaves across the range of selectivities has not been measured. A predicate that implements SizedIdFilter also says how many ids it allows: when that count is at most ef, the tier scans the allowed ids exactly and does not walk, and TieredIndex.liveCount is the number to compare the count with. A wrong count never lets a rejected id through. exists today: SizedIdFilterTest. The threshold is not set from a study (#12).
  • Context. The library calls expired() on the searching thread: when the search starts, before each tail and each segment, at least once every 1024 candidates inside a tail scan or a segment search (a candidate is a vector that the scan or the graph walk looks at, whether or not the predicate accepts it), and after each pause while it waits for a batch. When the answer is true the search throws SearchCancelledException and returns nothing. A context that returns true from partialWanted() gets a partial result on that exception (partialHits()): at most k hits, best first, with exact scores, of the tails and segments that were read to the end, so the source in progress is left out. It holds no deleted id and no stale vector, and it is empty when a batch was applied during the search. The time to stop is therefore up to one interval of candidates with their predicate calls, and a call of the predicate or of expired() is never interrupted. The method must be cheap, must not block, and must not call into the index. The standalone indexes take no context. exists today: SearchContext, TieredIndex.search. Tests: SearchContextTest (the bound in the tail scan, the graph walk and the exact scan of a segment, the poll before each part, equal answers while the context never expires, a flag set by another thread, a search that waits for a batch) and PartialResultTest.
  • Threads and locks. A search runs on the calling thread, takes no lock, and never waits for a seal, a merge, or the build of a rebuild. It can be delayed by a batch in progress, for the length of that batch (it waits until the batch is whole, and scans again when a batch overlapped its scan; see apply(batch)), and by the swap of a snapshot rebuild together with its catch-up. A stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve it. partly: built in TieredIndex.search and stated in its class documentation, and ApplyBatchTest checks the wait for a batch, but no dedicated test checks the rest.
  • Freshness. By default a search sees the tails, so a write is visible at once. Freshness.SEALED_ONLY skips the tails and may lag. It never returns a deleted id, a stale vector, or an id that was never added. exists today: TieredIndex.Freshness.

docs.title: Visibility and publish
docs.text:
• The writing transaction sees its own uncommitted rows through the host's overlay. Any other session sees nothing before commit. After commit, the batch is visible from the moment apply returns. A host that calls apply before it tells its client the commit is done gives that client read-your-writes. The overlay is the adapter's job, see the last section.
  • The segment list, the active tail, and the frozen tail live in one immutable view. A seal or a merge publishes a new view with one volatile write, and a search reads the view once. exists today: the view inside TieredIndex.
  • An in-flight search finishes on the view it read, and retired segments stay valid until the last reader leaves. In memory, garbage collection does that. partly: there is no dedicated test of a long search across a swap. A memory-mapped reader would need a reference count before it unmaps, and none is planned yet.
  • Seal and merge never block a search, and block add, delete, and apply only for a short critical section. exists today for seal, merge, and rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long), whose swap holds the write lock for the catch-up (EpochReplayTest.writesThatArriveDuringTheBuildAreKeptAndAppliedAfterTheSwap lets a write from another thread through during the build). partly for the one-argument rebuildFrom(Iterable), which holds the write lock for the whole build.
  • Close with searches in flight: later calls throw ClosedException, and an in-flight search finishes or throws it, never returning a wrong id. exists today: TieredIndex.close, tested by HostContractTest.callsAfterCloseThrowClosedException and HostContractTest.aSearchThatRunsWhileTheIndexClosesFinishesWithACorrectAnswer.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Open: the host opens after its own recovery has finished, so the records and ids it exposes are final. The result is ready or cold.
  • Readiness: a cold index is built from the record source, on the host executor, under a host permit.
  • Rebuild from records: always available, and always correct, because the vectors in the host's records are the truth. It is the answer to every integrity failure.
  • Flush, close, drop, clear, and verify: as in the operations table.
  • Files: a host may keep the library's files outside its own storage. The library never registers a file with the host's storage manager, writes only inside the directory it is given, and treats a restored or replicated copy that has no files as a cold index. planned (#9).
  • Persistence: the format, as the first cut writes it, is in SEGMENT-FORMAT.md. A tier with an empty tail is written by TieredIndex.checkpoint and read by TieredIndex.open, with the rows that deletes and replaces have hidden. The tests for damaged files and crashes at scale are #17.

docs.title: Recovery
docs.text:
• After a restart the host replays what the persisted state lacks, and the library reconciles what the host deleted or never made durable. The steps, the high-water id, the liveness check, and the durable-prefix rule are in ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. exists today for a process kill: EpochReplayTest.aCrashAtEveryStepOfAPublishLeavesAnIndexThatMatchesTheHost and EpochReplayStressTest.crashAndReopenLoop.
  • Requirement on the host, write-ahead: the index is never ahead of the host's durable log. A checkpoint may cover only transactions that the host has already made durable. If the library persisted a delete (a compacted segment) that the host then forgot in a crash, the record is live again in the host with an id at or below the recovered maximum and no segment holds it, and no rule of the library repairs that. The library cannot check the requirement, so a host that calls checkpoint before its own flush has a host error; the host that flushes first never sees the case. A library-side refusal to persist an unconfirmed delete is not built. exists today as a requirement; the test host of EpochReplayStressTest follows it.
  • Any integrity failure at open throws, and the host calls rebuildFrom. A second failure is a host error. exists today: TieredIndex.open(dir, config) throws the unchecked CorruptStateException for damage, with the SegmentFormat.CorruptException as its cause (a newer format, another index definition, and a missing manifest stay checked: UnsupportedException, MismatchException, NoSuchFileException), and the overloads with a rebuild source do the fallback (TierCorruptionTest).
  • The claim: a process kill leaves the last published generation or the one before it. No claim is made about power loss until a test says otherwise. exists today for a process kill: ManifestCrashTest, TierReopenTest, and TierHaltTest, which halts a child JVM at each step of a publish (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md). Crashes at scale: #17.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• No thread of the library's own. Every seal, merge, and build task, including the parallel part of a build, goes to the host executor. exists today with a HostEnv: HostEnvTest.aHostedTierCreatesNoThreadAndAsksForAPermitBeforeEveryBuild compares the live threads before and after a workload that seals and merges. A tier without one starts its own threads. A rebuild still runs on the calling thread.
  • Build permit. Before each seal, merge, and rebuild the library asks for a permit with an estimate of peak bytes, computed from the sizes involved. On refusal it defers and retries with back-off, and never builds without a permit; a call that builds on its own thread throws BuildRefusedException. The retry needs the timer of the host (HostEnv.schedule) or its call of maintain() when no write comes. exists today: HostEnvTest. partly for the estimate: it is arithmetic and has not been compared with a measured peak (#13).
  • Memory budget. The library defers merges and shrinks its tail limit to stay below the budget. partly: HostEnvTest.aSmallMemoryBudgetShrinksTheTailDefersMergesAndKeepsTheBytesBelowIt holds the resident bytes below the budget for data that fits in it. The budget cannot shrink what the vectors need, and it does not hold writes back.
  • Throttle. The insert rate of a merge build is capped (Config.mergeRatePerSec). It is a politeness limit for the threads that serve queries, not a substitute for a permit. partly: built, and no dedicated test checks the cap.
  • Back pressure is a pre-check (awaitCapacity), and the tail is bounded. partly: TieredIndex.awaitCapacity is built and tested. The bound is soft: apply does not look at it, so one batch can take the tail above the hard limit, and TieredIndex.add adds after its own wait of up to 10 s.
  • No search-time thread creation, and no allocation proportional to the collection size on the query path. partly: built in TieredIndex.search, and no dedicated test checks it.
  • The graph kernels need the jdk.incubator.vector module at run time. The graph kernels have a scalar twin that is used when the module is absent, exists today: KernDiffTest compares the vector and the scalar kernel, and NoIncubatorTest builds and searches a tier in a JVM without the module. A native-image build of the library and a smoke program is checked by the workflow native-image.yml (the job native image smoke, and the vector variant native image smoke (vector, ...) on x86-64 and arm64 Linux), exists today, not a required check. In a native image the graph kernels (dot, squared L2, and the SQ8 dot) use the Vector API through NKernels with a build-time species, and a score can differ from the JVM by rounding.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
• The library reads its configuration from a Map<String, String> and gives a fingerprint. The fingerprint is a canonical string and a hash over the data-affecting settings only: dimension, metric, id width, graph parameters (M, efConstruction, alpha), segment quantization, and layer layout. Search-time knobs (the beam width, the split-beam switch), the settings of the tail (it is not persisted), the maintenance policy, and the random seed are not part of it. exists today: Config.toMap, Config.fromMap, Config.fingerprint (HostContractTest).
  • The host stores the fingerprint in its index metadata and compares it before it opens the persisted state. On a mismatch it builds from its records. open itself discards state of another dimension, metric, M, efConstruction, or SQ8 setting; the files do not record alpha. exists today on the library side.
  • Unknown keys are rejected at creation with the key named, and ignored with a warning at load, so a downgrade still opens. exists today: Config.fromMap, Config.fromStoredMap (HostContractTest).
  • Search-time knobs may change at run time. Data-affecting keys may not. exists today: TieredIndex.reconfigure (HostContractTest.onlyTheSearchTimeKnobsChangeInAnOpenIndex).
  • The keys are listed in DESIGN.md.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
• A pull form: a Map<String, Long> of counters and gauges. A push form: a sink with counter(name) and gauge(name, supplier). Names are prefixed tiervec.. No metrics library is a dependency. exists today: TieredIndex.metrics, TieredIndex.bindMetrics, MetricSink (HostContractTest).
  • The quantities are the ones TieredIndex.Stats holds: seals, merges, failures, back-pressure waits, tail size, segment count, bytes held, floor entries, and write amplification (a gauge in thousandths). The names are in DESIGN.md.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Errors for the state of an index are unchecked. The base is TiervecException. Classes: CorruptStateException (the host falls back to rebuildFrom), SearchCancelledException, ClosedException, and BuildRefusedException. Programming errors stay IllegalArgumentException and IllegalStateException, and a failure of the file system stays an IOException. exists today; BuildRefusedException comes from a tier with a HostEnv only.
  • A background failure never throws into apply or search. It is counted, kept as the last error, and retried. A health state reports ok, degraded (a seal or a merge that failed three times in a row), or failed (the worker is dead). exists today: TieredIndex.health, TieredIndex.lastError, Stats.failures (HostContractTest).

docs.title: Versioning and capabilities
docs.text:
• The contract has a major and a minor number, 1.0 today. The host refuses a library with a larger major. A larger minor is accepted, and capabilities it does not know are ignored. New operations are added as default methods. exists today: TieredIndex.contractVersion, ContractVersion.accepts (HostContractTest).
  • The segment file and the manifest have their own version numbers, under the same rule. planned (#6, #9).
  • Capabilities are a set (EnumSet, a bit set): atomic batch, deferred apply, search context, persistence, snapshot rebuild, host environment, and selective filter plan, with more as they appear. The host checks them at creation. exists today: TieredIndex.capabilities, Capability.
  • What the tier does not offer, so a host can refuse such an index definition at creation and not at query time: grouped (per-group top k) search, approximate scores from compressed codes without an exact rescoring pass (returned scores are exact fp32 scores), a retract of an applied write other than the opposite write, transactions or uncommitted rows, a persisted tail, memory-mapped segment readers, and more than one process on one index directory. exists today as a fact about the code.

docs.title: What a host adapter typically does
docs.text:
The adapter is the host's code. It sits between the host's classes and the library, and it is where the host's own concepts end.

  • Key mapping. The adapter keeps a table from library id to the host's record handle, and mints a new id for every new vector version. A hit costs one lookup in that table. An update sends an add of the new id and a delete of the old id in one batch.
  • Overlay of uncommitted rows. The library has no transaction notion. For a search inside an open transaction, the adapter scores that transaction's pending rows exactly, with the same metric, merges them with the library's hits by score, and masks the ids the transaction has superseded by excluding them in the allowed-id predicate.
  • Allowed-id bridging. The host's filter produces a set of record handles. The adapter wraps it as a LongPredicate over library ids: map the id to its record handle, then test membership. It passes a size hint when it knows one.
  • Staging. The adapter holds a transaction's adds and deletes until the changes stand, then calls apply once.
  • Recovery glue. The adapter implements the record source on top of the host's own record scan and id table, and persists the epoch beside its own data.
  • Conversion. If the host reports distances where lower is better, the adapter converts scores, and a parity test on the same data checks the conversion.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page is the rule for version numbers and the steps of a release. The first release is 0.1.0. Between releases the version on main is the next -SNAPSHOT.

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text:
• A release version is 0.MINOR.PATCH while the API is not stable. At 1.0 it becomes MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.
  • A breaking change to the supported surface needs a new MINOR version. A release that has none can be a new PATCH version. The rule and the meaning of "breaking" are in API.md.
  • Between releases main carries a -SNAPSHOT version, as Maven expects. After 0.1.0, main is 0.1.1-SNAPSHOT. When the first breaking change lands, main moves to 0.2.0-SNAPSHOT.
  • There is no .devN, aN, bN or rcN form. Maven does not order 0.1.0-dev1 before 0.1.0: it sorts an unknown qualifier after the release. A pre-release is a -SNAPSHOT.
  • A tag is the bare version, for example 0.1.0, with no v.
  • The version has one source: the <version> line in pom.xml.

docs.title: What a release has
docs.text:
• A tag on the commit of main that carries the release version.
  • A section in CHANGELOG.md with the version and the date.
  • A GitHub release whose notes are that section.
  • A documentation version <version> with the alias latest at https://docs.humem.ai/tiervec/. The tag push publishes it (workflow deploy-docs.yml). A push to main publishes only dev.
  • The artifact ai.humem:tiervec:<version> on Maven Central: the jar, a sources jar and a javadoc jar, each signed. Publishing the GitHub release starts everything (workflow release-central.yml): the upload, the publication by the Central Portal, and a check of the result on repo1.maven.org. Nobody presses a button in the portal. The details are in the section "Maven Central" below (#62).

docs.title: The changelog
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md follows the "Keep a Changelog" layout: a section Unreleased at the top, then one section per release, newest first. The groups in a section are Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed and Security.

A pull request that changes the supported surface, the file format, or a documented guarantee adds its line to Unreleased in the same pull request. A breaking change says so and says what to change. A change in the file format says which older readers refuse the new files (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md).

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Only the maintainer tags and publishes a release.

  1. Check that the latest commit on main is green: every check of its run is SUCCESS (a skipped check is fine). Do not release from a red or running main. The slow tests (slow tests (JDK 21) and slow tests (JDK 25), workflow slow-tests.yml) and the arm64 fast tests (workflow ci.yml) are among these checks: every push to main starts them. The native image jobs start only on a push that changes the library, the smoke program or their workflow file, so the latest commit may not have them. Check that the newest run on main is green too: gh run list --workflow native-image.yml --branch main --limit 1.
  2. Create the branch release/<version> from that commit.
  3. In pom.xml, change <version> to the release version (no -SNAPSHOT).
  4. In CHANGELOG.md, rename Unreleased to <version> - YYYY-MM-DD, add an empty Unreleased above it, and read the entry once against git log <previous tag>..HEAD.
  5. Update docs/STATUS.md and the README status table where the release changes what they say (for example the line "A release: none").
  6. Run the Central dry run on the branch and read its result (see "Maven Central" below):
gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref release/<version> -f dry-run=true
  1. Open a pull request named Release <version> and add the label ci:slow to it, so that the slow tests run on it (a pull request without the label skips them). The arm64 fast tests run on it too, because the branch name starts with release/. Wait for green, the two slow jobs and the three arm64 jobs included, and merge it.
  2. The merge is a push to main, and it starts the slow tests on the merge commit, which is the commit of the release. Wait for that run to end green (gh run list --workflow slow-tests.yml --commit <merge-sha>). Then tag the merge commit and push the tag. The tag is the bare version:
git tag <version> <merge-sha>
git push origin <version>

The tag push starts the workflow Deploy docs. It publishes the documentation as <version> with the alias latest, and latest is the default of the site.

  1. Publish the GitHub release. The notes are the changelog section of this version:
gh release create <version> --title <version> --notes-file <file with the section>

Publishing the release is the last manual act. It starts the workflow Release to Maven Central, which does the rest.

  1. Wait for the workflow Release to Maven Central to finish green:

    gh run list --workflow release-central.yml --limit 1
gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status

    It builds from the tag, signs, uploads the bundle, lets the Central Portal publish it, waits for the files on repo1.maven.org and verifies them (the section "The publish run" below has the list). There is nothing to press in the portal. A green run means that ai.humem:tiervec:<version> resolves from Maven Central, which is the done-when of issue #62: the first green run comments on that issue and closes it. A red run is read in its log; "The publish run" says what each failure means. 11. In a second pull request, set <version> on main to the next -SNAPSHOT (see above).

A tag is never moved or deleted. A mistake in a release is fixed by the next PATCH release, and the changelog says so. A version on Maven Central cannot be changed or removed once it is published.

docs.title: Maven Central
docs.text:
The artifact is ai.humem:tiervec. The namespace ai.humem is verified on the Central Portal (https://central.sonatype.com), account taewoon@humem.ai. Central accepts the artifact only with a complete pom.xml (name, description, url, license, developers, scm), a sources jar, a javadoc jar and a GnuPG signature on every file. The profile release in pom.xml builds and signs all of that, and the plugin central-publishing-maven-plugin uploads one bundle. The profile does not publish by default: the property central.autoPublish is false in pom.xml, so a local build and the dry run stop at VALIDATED or before. Only the publish run of the workflow passes -Dcentral.autoPublish=true -Dcentral.waitUntil=published, and then the Portal publishes the deployment as soon as it is valid. Creating the GitHub release is the deliberate act that starts it, and a published version cannot be taken back.

Only the workflow release-central.yml runs the profile with real credentials. Nobody runs it from a laptop.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Four repository secrets of humemai/tiervec (Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions). The workflow reads nothing else.

Name What it holds CENTRAL_USERNAME The user name of the Central Portal user token CENTRAL_PASSWORD The password of the same token GPG_PRIVATE_KEY The armored private signing key GPG_PASSPHRASE The passphrase of that key

Check that the four names exist (the values cannot be read, and the command shows names only):

gh api repos/humemai/tiervec/actions/secrets --jq '[.secrets[].name]'

The workflow never prints a value, never puts one on a command line and never writes one to a file. The settings.xml it creates has ${env.CENTRAL_USERNAME} and ${env.CENTRAL_PASSWORD} references, mode 600, in the runner temp directory, and it removes the file and the GnuPG home at the end.

docs.title: The signing key
docs.text:
Create a key (a second key is not needed if one exists), store it as secrets without printing it, and publish the public key. <FPR> is the fingerprint that gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long shows.

gpg --quick-generate-key "HumemAI tiervec releases <taewoon@humem.ai>" ed25519 sign 3y
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format long taewoon@humem.ai

gpg --armor --export-secret-keys <FPR> | gh secret set GPG_PRIVATE_KEY --repo humemai/tiervec
gh secret set GPG_PASSPHRASE --repo humemai/tiervec

gpg --keyserver hkps://keyserver.ubuntu.com --send-keys <FPR>
gpg --armor --export <FPR> > tiervec-release-key.asc

gh secret set GPG_PASSPHRASE asks for the value, so it does not reach the shell history. Upload tiervec-release-key.asc at https://keys.openpgp.org/upload and follow the link in the e-mail it sends, then delete the file. Central looks the public key up on these key servers when it validates a signature, so a deployment fails validation until the key is published.

The token pair comes from the portal (Account, Generate User Token). Store it the same way, each command asks for its value:

gh secret set CENTRAL_USERNAME --repo humemai/tiervec
gh secret set CENTRAL_PASSWORD --repo humemai/tiervec

docs.title: Dry run
docs.text:
gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref <branch or main> -f dry-run=true
gh run list --workflow release-central.yml --limit 1
gh run view <run-id> --log-failed

The dry run is the default of the manual trigger and runs on any branch (GitHub dispatches a workflow only when its file is on main). It also runs on every pull request that changes pom.xml, src/main or the workflow file, so a Javadoc error or a broken release profile shows up in the pull request and not at release time; that check is not required. It generates a throwaway signing key inside the job, so it needs no secret and has no Central credentials: it cannot publish. It exports that key and imports it into a second GnuPG home with the script .github/scripts/import-signing-key.sh, the same script the publish run uses, so the import from an environment variable and the signing with a passphrase are rehearsed. It builds with JDK 21 (-Prelease -DskipTests, with a -SNAPSHOT version written as its release form in the job's checkout, because the Central plugin writes a bundle only for a release version), signs, writes the Central bundle, and then checks the bundle: the jar, sources jar, javadoc jar and pom are all there with checksums and a valid signature, the sources jar and the javadoc jar have content, and the pom has the elements Central requires. It uploads the bundle as the run artifact central-dry-run-bundle (7 days).

The dry run also checks and tests the scripts of the publish run: bash -n and shellcheck on every script in .github/scripts, and .github/scripts/test-central-scripts.sh. That test runs verify-central-release.sh and check-central-absent.sh against a local server that stands in for repo1.maven.org and the key server, throwaway signing keys and a Maven stub, so it needs nothing from the network. Each case spoils one thing (a flipped byte, a missing .asc, a wrong checksum, a bad signature, a signature of another key, a key that cannot be fetched, a jar that is not the built jar, a version that never appears) and the script must fail with the message of that thing; the good set must pass. To run it on a laptop: PYTHON_BIN="$(uv run --no-project python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)')" bash .github/scripts/test-central-scripts.sh.

It does not prove that the real key, the passphrase and the token work, or that the key is on a key server. The publish run checks the first two early: it imports the key with the same script, signs a probe file with the passphrase, and stops before the build if that fails.

The dry run covers what changes with the code, such as a Javadoc error. Run it on the release branch before the tag (step 6).

docs.title: The publish run
docs.text:
The run starts when a GitHub release is published, or by hand with -f dry-run=false on the tag. Creating the release is the deliberate act: nothing else starts a publish. It refuses to run unless the ref is a tag that equals the version in pom.xml (a bare version, no -SNAPSHOT), the tagged commit is on main, the version is not on Maven Central yet, and all four secrets are present. "Not on Central yet" means that https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/ai/humem/tiervec/<version>/ answers 404, so a re-run cannot push a duplicate. An answer that is neither 404 nor 200 stops the run too, because "cannot tell" must not mean "go on".

What the run does, in order:

  1. Checks the tag, the pom version, that the commit is on main, that the version is not on Central, and the four secrets.
  2. Imports the signing key with .github/scripts/import-signing-key.sh and signs a probe file, so a wrong passphrase fails before the build. It keeps the fingerprint of the key (a public value) for step 6.
  3. Builds with the profile release and the fast tests, signs the jar, the sources jar, the javadoc jar and the pom, and uploads the bundle to the Central Portal. An expired Central token shows up here as an HTTP 401.
  4. The Portal validates the bundle and, because the run passes -Dcentral.autoPublish=true -Dcentral.waitUntil=published, publishes it. The Central plugin waits until the deployment is PUBLISHED, for at most central.waitMaxTime (3600 seconds).
  5. Waits for the sync from the Portal to repo1.maven.org: it polls https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/ai/humem/tiervec/<version>/tiervec-<version>.pom every 30 seconds, for at most 60 minutes, and fails with the last answer when the file never appears. (The search index of https://central.sonatype.com and search.maven.org is slower than the repository; the check uses repo1.maven.org only.)
  6. Verifies the result with .github/scripts/verify-central-release.sh: it downloads the jar, the sources jar, the javadoc jar and the pom with their .asc and checksum files; checks md5, sha1 and sha256 (and sha512 where served) against the bytes; fetches the public key from keyserver.ubuntu.com by the fingerprint of step 2 and checks that every signature is valid and made by that key; compares the three jars byte for byte with the jars that step 3 built, so what is on Central is what was built; and resolves ai.humem:tiervec:<version> with dependency:get in an empty local Maven repository with an isolated settings file (no mirrors, Central only).
  7. Writes the result in the job summary. The first version that passes also comments on issue #62 and closes it. A later version has no issue to comment on (releases are tracked by milestone, and a milestone or a GitHub release takes no comment), so the job summary and the run are its record.

To see it: gh run watch <run-id> --exit-status follows the run, and the job summary has the table of what Central serves. The Portal shows the deployment read-only at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments; there is nothing to press there.

What a failure means:

  • Red in step 3 with an HTTP 401: the Central token expired or is wrong. Rotate it (issue #97, the reminder below) and run the workflow again on the same tag.
  • Red in step 3 or 4 because the deployment is FAILED: nothing was published. Read the messages in the portal, drop the deployment, fix the cause, and run the workflow again on the same tag (gh workflow run release-central.yml --ref <version> -f dry-run=false). Fixing a problem in the sources needs a new version, because a tag is never moved.
  • Red in step 5 or 6: the version is published and is not taken back, whatever the verification said. If the pom never appeared within 60 minutes, run the workflow Verify on Maven Central (below) later. If a checksum, a signature or a jar differs, that is a real defect of the release: the fix is the next patch version, and its changelog says so.
  • A deployment that sits at VALIDATED (the run was stopped, or it was started with auto-publish set to false): press Publish for ai.humem:tiervec:<version> at https://central.sonatype.com/publishing/deployments, then run Verify on Maven Central. Do not run the publish run again while that deployment is in the portal: drop it first, because the check "not on Central yet" cannot see a deployment that is not synced.
  • To choose the manual path from the start, run the workflow by hand on the tag with -f dry-run=false -f auto-publish=false. It uploads, waits for VALIDATED and stops without publishing, the run summary says so, and the steps above for a deployment at VALIDATED apply. A release event always auto-publishes.

docs.title: Verify on Maven Central
docs.text:
The workflow Verify on Maven Central (verify-central.yml) runs the same verification for a version that is already out, with no secret and no write permission:

gh workflow run verify-central.yml -f version=<version> -f fingerprint=<FPR>

<FPR> is the 40 hex digits of the signing key: the line signing key fingerprint: in the log of the publish run, or gpg --list-keys --with-colons for the key on a laptop. It cannot compare the jars with a build, because it has none. Use it after a manual Publish, after a publish run that timed out while waiting, and to check an old version again.

docs.title: Reminder: the Central token expires
docs.text: The Central user token was created on 2026-11-12 with an expiry of one year, so it expires around 2027-11. Rotate it before then: generate a new token in the portal, set CENTRAL_USERNAME and CENTRAL_PASSWORD again, and keep the date of the new expiry here. An expired token shows as an authentication error (HTTP 401) in the upload step of the publish run, and the dry run cannot catch it because it uses no token. If the signing key has an expiry (the example above has three years), that date is a second rotation point: extend it with gpg --edit-key <FPR> expire, export it again as above and upload the public key again.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

The order of work follows one question: what does a database that embeds this index need from it? The list is ordered by that need. It has no dates. Each item is a GitHub issue with a problem statement, an acceptance test, and an explicit out-of-scope list. What exists today is in STATUS.md, and the architecture is in DESIGN.md.

docs.title: What a host needs
docs.text:
A host is the database that runs the index in its own process. These are the properties that decide whether an index fits a host, as opposed to fitting a benchmark:

  • A committed vector is found by the next query, exactly, also across a seal, a merge, or a swap.
  • Update and delete stay correct when the host reuses a record id.
  • A batch of adds and deletes becomes visible as a unit.
  • The index survives a crash and reopens without a full rebuild, and a damaged file is detected, never trusted.
  • A filter from the host's query language (an allowed set of ids) is fast and correct at every selectivity.
  • Memory is bounded, and the host, not the index, owns threads, build concurrency, and the memory budget.
  • Rebuild and merge cost does not stall queries while writes continue.
  • Small and medium collections work well by default, with few knobs.
  • It runs on the JVM and in a native image.

docs.title: Now
docs.text:
Decisions and tests that the rest of the work depends on.

  • #4: Choose the default merge policy: one large segment plus a small recent one
  • #5: Tests for record-id reuse and tombstone correctness across seal and merge
  • #6: Specify the segment file and the manifest
  • #7: Define the id epoch and the replay protocol for a host. Page: ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md. The epoch, the snapshot rebuild, and the replay in open are built, see STATUS.md.
  • #8: Document the host contract in docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md. Page: PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Library work that follows from the items above. CI already runs the fast and the slow tests on JDK 21 and 25, so there is no separate item for that.

  • #9: Serialize sealed segments with a manifest, and reopen without a full rebuild. First cut: SEGMENT-FORMAT.md. Memory-mapped readers and lazy verification are not in it; they are tracked in #27. Tombstones for deleted and replaced ids are built. The host replays the tail through open with a record source (#7).
  • #10: Atomic apply(batch): adds and deletes become visible together. TieredIndex.apply and TieredIndex.awaitCapacity are built, see STATUS.md.
  • #11: Search context with a deadline and cancellation. SearchContext is built, see STATUS.md.
  • #12: Allowed-id filters: measure the selectivity range and add fast paths. The size hint (SizedIdFilter) and liveCount are built; the study that sets the thresholds is not done.
  • #13: Host-owned executor, build permits, and memory budget instead of own threads. HostEnv is built, see DESIGN.md. The estimate of the merge peak has not been compared with measurements.
  • #18: Configuration map, fingerprint, capability bits, and contract version. Config.toMap, fromMap, fingerprint, reconfigure, contractVersion, capabilities, metrics, health, and the unchecked exceptions are built, see DESIGN.md.
  • #14: Scalar twin of the graph kernel. Kern follows the same once-per-JVM switch as the flat kernels, so the graph and the tier also run without the Vector API module.
  • #15: Native-image build and smoke test in CI. The job native image smoke builds an image of the library with a small program that covers the flat, IVF, graph, and tiered indexes without the Vector API and compares every answer with an exact scan; the jobs native image smoke (vector, ...) do the same with the fp32 dot and squared L2 (#44) and the int8, SQ8, and block16 kernels (#48) on the Vector API. Segment files and concurrent writers are not in it.
