docs.title: Later
docs.text:
One tracking issue with a checklist: #19: Later: work that waits until the host contract holds

It covers 1-bit and 4-bit quantization schemes, IVF as a segment format, an on-disk graph, and other language bindings. Each item becomes its own issue when it is promoted.

docs.title: How to read measurements
docs.text: The harness is in the repository (BENCHMARKS.md), and no measurement is published yet. A single run (n=1) is descriptive: it shows what happened, not what usually happens. A claim of a 1.3x difference or larger needs at least five runs, each in a fresh JVM, and a smaller difference needs more. Every study states its claim, its arms, its number of runs, and the bound it must meet before it runs. Memory figures say which unit and which counter they use, and latency figures say whether the JIT was warm.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A server. The index is a library that runs in the host's process, with no network between the host and the index.
  • A query language. The host parses SQL, Cypher, or anything else, and hands the index vectors and allowed-id sets.
  • Its own persistence of records. The host's records are the source of truth, and everything the index stores is derived and can be rebuilt from them.
  • GPU index builds or search.

docs.title: Segment files and the manifest
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

This page describes what the code writes and reads today (the first cut of #9). A tier with an empty tail is written to a directory with TieredIndex.checkpoint(dir) and read back with TieredIndex.open(dir, config). One sealed graph can also be written alone with SealedGraph.serialize(file) and read with SealedGraph.load(file).

The records of the host stay the source of truth. Everything in the directory is derived data that can be deleted and rebuilt with TieredIndex.rebuildFrom. When open cannot trust the directory, it throws, and the host rebuilds from its records.

The claim the format makes: a process kill at any point of a publish leaves generation N or generation N+1 of the directory, plus files that the next open removes. No claim is made about power loss (see "What a crash leaves behind").

docs.title: Files in an index directory
docs.text:
File What it holds seg-<id>.tvs One immutable segment: the arrays of one SealedGraph. The id is zero-padded to at least six digits. tomb-<generation>.tvd The tombstone bitmaps of every segment of a generation: the rows that a delete or a replace has hidden. manifest-<generation>.tvm One generation: the live segments, the tombstone file, a configuration fingerprint. The generation is zero-padded to 20 digits. *.tmp A file being written. Never named by a manifest. Removed at open. LOCK An empty file whose operating system lock says which process owns the directory (see "One process per directory"). Never deleted.

Nothing that a manifest names is ever modified. A new state is a new manifest and, when needed, new segment files.

docs.title: One process per directory
docs.text:
checkpoint and every open take an exclusive lock on LOCK before they read or write anything else in the directory, and the tier keeps it until close, or until a checkpoint into another directory has succeeded. A second process gets DirectoryLockedException, which names the directory, and nothing there changes. This includes the open overloads with a rebuild source: they do not rebuild, because two owners of one directory would delete each other's files. The tiers of one process share the lock, and it is released when the last of them lets go.

The lock is the operating system's, so it ends with the process, however the process ends, and there is no stale lock to remove. On Windows it can end a moment after the process has: an open right after a process was killed can throw DirectoryLockedException, and a host that restarts at once tries again (seen in TierKillLongTest on the Windows runner; the documentation of LockFileEx gives no bound for the release). Do not delete the file while a process uses the directory. No lock is taken on a file system other than the default one, or in a directory that the process cannot write to. Whether the lock holds between machines on a network file system depends on that file system, and nothing here tests it. A version before this one neither takes nor checks the lock.

docs.title: Segment file
docs.text:
All numbers are little-endian. The file is, in order:

[0, 4096)                 header block
[4096, ...)               sections, each starting at a multiple of the alignment, in table order
[F, F + footer length)    footer: metadata and the section table
[end - 32, end)           locator

The header block holds nothing that depends on the section bytes, and the CRCs live in the footer, so a writer streams the file from front to back and never goes back.

docs.title: Header block
docs.text:
Offset Size Field 0 8 magic TVSEG001 8 2 major version 10 2 minor version 12 4 header length (52 in this version; the last 4 bytes of the header are its CRC) 16 4 byte-order probe 0x01020304 20 4 flags (none defined) 24 4 dim 28 4 stride_floats (equal to dim in this version; rows are not padded) 32 8 n, the number of rows 40 1 metric code: 0 cosine, 1 dot, 2 L2 41 1 id width in bytes (8) 42 1 layer 0 layout (0 is CSR, offsets plus edges) 43 1 reserved 44 4 section alignment (4096) 48 4 CRC32C of bytes 0 to 47 52 4044 zero fill, not covered by the CRC

Enums are stored as explicit codes, never as ordinals.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Every section is a plain array of one fixed-width type. Each starts at a multiple of the alignment; the bytes between the end of one section and the start of the next are zero and are not covered by any CRC.

Id Name Element Count Notes 1 IDS i64 n Id of each row, in row order. Required. 2 VERS i64 n Version of each row, written by the tier. Optional for a standalone graph. 3 BYID i32 n Rows in increasing id order. A load uses it as is and does not sort. Required. 4 VEC f32 n * dim The fp32 vectors (unit length when the metric is cosine). Required. 5 LEVEL u8 n Top layer of each row. Required. 6 L0_OFF i32 n + 1 CSR offsets of layer 0. Required. 7 L0_EDGES i32 L0_OFF[n] Layer 0 neighbor rows. Required. 8 UP_IDX i32 n Index into UP_OFF for rows above layer 0, -1 otherwise. Required. 9 UP_OFF i32 free Offsets of the upper layers. Required. 10 UP_EDGES i32 free Neighbor rows of the upper layers. Required. 11 SQ8_CODES i8 n * dim Present when the graph has SQ8 codes. 12 SQ8_PARAMS f32 3 * n qbase, then qdelta, then qnorm. Present with section 11, never alone.

Section ids are never reused. The REQUIRED flag (bit 0 of the section flags) is set on the sections a reader cannot do without, and matters only for ids a reader does not know.

docs.title: Footer
docs.text:
The footer starts with 64 bytes of metadata, then one 40-byte entry per section.

Offset Size Field 0 4 entry row of the graph 4 4 top level 8 4 M 12 4 efConstruction 16 4 efSearch (a default for searches, not part of the data) 20 4 alpha (f32) 24 8 seed 32 8 smallest row version (0 when there is no VERS) 40 8 largest row version 48 4 flags: bit 0 is the SQ8 parameter flag 52 4 number of sections 56 4 offset of the first section entry (64 in this version) 60 4 reserved

A section entry is: id u16, flags u16, element width u32, element count u64, offset u64, length u64, CRC32C u32, reserved u32. The CRC covers exactly the section bytes.

docs.title: Locator
docs.text: The last 32 bytes: magic TVSEGEND (8), footer offset u64, footer length u32, footer CRC32C u32, total file length u64. The locator is the last thing written. A file that was cut short, or that has bytes appended, does not end in a locator that agrees with its own length, and fails after reading 32 bytes.

docs.title: Sizes
docs.text: The file holds the arrays of the in-memory graph, with VERS and BYID in place of the two sorted-id arrays the graph keeps, and no deletion bitmap. So, with VERS present, the sum of the section lengths equals SealedGraph.bytesHeld() minus 8 * ceil(n / 64) (the bitmap). The file length is 4096, plus the sections each rounded up to the alignment, plus 64 + 40 * sections, plus 32. SegmentFormatTest checks both for two dimensions, with and without SQ8.

docs.title: Integrity rules
docs.text:
• A reader reads the header block, the locator and the footer first, and checks the magic, the header CRC, the version, the byte-order probe, the locator against the real file length, and the footer CRC. This costs the same for a file of any size and happens before any section is read.
  • The section table is checked: offsets aligned, ascending, inside the file, element width times count equal to the length, the width and count of every known section as expected, all required sections present.
  • SegmentReader.read(file, true) also checks the CRC32C of every section and names the section that failed (CorruptException.section()). SealedGraph.load and TieredIndex.open always do. read(file, false) skips the section CRCs and is meant for inspection.
  • The stored id order is checked while it is used (rows in range, ids strictly increasing), and the layer 0 offsets are checked against the edge count.
  • A magic that is not TVSEG001 is damage. The magic is the same in every version (the version is the major and minor fields after it), so a file that does not start with it is refused with CorruptException (section HEADER), and the message names the file and the field. TieredIndex.open treats such a segment like any other damaged one: see "Open".
  • A CRC32C detects accidental damage. It is not protection against tampering.

docs.title: Versioning and compatibility
docs.text:
A segment file has a format version major.minor.

  • The header frame is the same in every version, newer major versions included: the magic in bytes 0 to 7, the major and minor version in bytes 8 to 11, the header length at offset 12, and a CRC32C of all header bytes before it in the last 4 bytes of the header, inside the 4096-byte header block. A reader checks that CRC before it believes the version.
  • A header whose CRC does not match is damage, whatever its version field says (CorruptException, section HEADER). A flipped bit in the version field is this case, and TieredIndex.open treats the segment like any other damaged one.
  • A reader refuses a file with an intact header and a larger major version (UnsupportedException). A major version of 0 with an intact header is refused the same way.
  • A header whose byte-order probe reads back swapped (0x04030201) is a big-endian header and is refused with UnsupportedException before the CRC, which does not read back in that case. No single flipped bit turns the probe into its swapped form.
  • A reader opens a file with a larger minor version. It ignores a section whose id it does not know, unless the section is marked required, in which case it refuses.
  • A newer minor may append header fields (the header length says where the header ends and where its CRC is) and footer metadata (the offset of the first section entry says where the table starts).
  • A different byte order, an id width other than 8, a layer 0 layout other than CSR, and a row stride other than dim are refused in this version.

The manifest and the tombstone file carry their own major.minor under the same rule. The frame of a manifest is the same in every version: the magic, the major and minor version, the body length at offset 12, and the CRC32C of the body in the last 4 bytes of the file. A reader checks the length and that CRC before it believes the version, so a damaged version field is CorruptException and only an intact manifest can be refused as newer. The tombstone file is compared with the length and CRC that the manifest holds before it is read. A manifest or a segment that an older reader does not understand is refused, not skipped: falling back to an older generation would silently serve stale data.

docs.title: Manifest and tombstone file
docs.text:
manifest-<generation>.tvm holds: magic TVMAN001, version, the body length, the generation, the epoch and the high-water id of the host (both "none" for a tier that never had an epoch; otherwise the host's epoch and the largest id that a segment holds), the version counter of the tier, the next free segment id, a fingerprint of the data-affecting configuration (dimension, metric, id width, M, efConstruction, whether SQ8 is on, the layer 0 layout), the generation, length and CRC of the tombstone file, one entry per live segment (id, row count, file length, the header CRC, smallest and largest row version), and a CRC32C of everything before it. File names are built from the ids in the manifest, never read from it.

tomb-<generation>.tvd holds: magic TVTOMB01, version, the generation, the number of segments, then for each segment its id, its row count and one bit per row (in 64-bit words, row r is bit r & 63 of word r >>> 6), and a CRC32C.

A set bit marks a row that a delete or a replace has hidden. The row stays in its segment file, which is never modified, until a merge rewrites the segment. Each generation has its own tombstone file, so a checkpoint that only deleted ids writes a new tombstone file and a new manifest and no segment. A reader refuses (CorruptException, section TOMBSTONES) a bit at or above the row count of its segment, and a file that leaves a row of an id visible while it marks a newer row of the same id: a tier hides older copies only.

Version 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 write only zero bits. They refuse a directory with a set bit with UnsupportedException, so their checkpoint does not overwrite it. A directory without a set bit has the same bytes as before.

docs.title: Publish
docs.text:
Manifest.publish makes a new generation live. The segment files it names are written and flushed first (SegmentWriter.write creates a new file and flushes it). Before the first generation of a directory, checkpoint makes the directory and the parents it lacks, one level at a time, and flushes each name into its parent; it flushes the name of the deepest directory that was already there too, because a killed checkpoint may have made it (when that parent may not be read, the name is left to whoever made the directory).

Step Action Hook point (FaultHook.Step) 1, 2 Write the segment files, flush each SEGMENTS_WRITTEN 3 Write and flush the tombstone file, flush the directory DIR_SYNCED_AFTER_SEGMENTS 4 Write the manifest under a temporary name MANIFEST_TMP_WRITTEN 5 Flush the temporary manifest MANIFEST_TMP_SYNCED 6 Rename it to manifest-<generation>.tvm MANIFEST_RENAMED 7 Flush the directory DIR_SYNCED_AFTER_RENAME 8 The caller switches its in-memory view, then Manifest.gc deletes what the new manifest does not name (none)

The rename is the only moment a generation becomes visible, and by then every byte it names was already flushed. Generation N is deleted only in step 8, after step 7, so an unfinished N+1 can exist only while N and all its files still exist. The cleanup (step 8, and the one at the end of open) flushes the directory before its first delete: an open that finds an N+1 whose process was killed between steps 6 and 7 makes that rename durable before it removes N. A manifest is never overwritten: publishing a generation that exists is an error.

On Windows the directory flush of steps 3 and 7 does nothing, because Java cannot open a directory there (FileChannel.open is refused). File contents are still forced with FileChannel.force, so the bytes of every file are flushed before the rename. The directory entry (the new name, the rename) is not flushed by the library, so a power loss right after a rename can lose the rename on Windows. A process kill is covered on Windows as on Linux, because the claim above is about process kills only.

docs.title: Guarantees per platform
docs.text:
These are the platforms that CI runs. "N or N+1" means that the directory opens as the generation before the publish or the new one, never a mixture.

Linux x86-64 Linux arm64 macOS arm64 Windows x64 File contents flushed before the rename (FileChannel.force) yes yes yes yes The rename itself flushed (directory flush) yes yes yes no A process kill during a publish leaves N or N+1 yes yes yes yes, and the lock of the killed process can be released a moment later A power loss no claim no claim no claim no claim, and a rename that has returned can be lost Tested by a child process halted at each publish step, and from the directories a power cut can leave (fast: TierHaltTest, TierPowerCutTest, ManifestCrashTest, TierReopenTest) every change every change every change every change Tested by many seeds and random process kills (slow: TierHaltLongTest, TierKillLongTest) slow runs no no slow runs Flush order tested on a simulated file system (SimulatedFsCrashTest) every change every change every change no, there is no directory flush to order

"Every change" is the fast tests of a pull request. "Slow runs" is a push to main, the daily run, and a pull request with the label ci:slow. None of these tests cuts the power. The library has no memory-mapped reader, so no file is mapped while a merge replaces it; what a mapped reader changes on Windows belongs to #27.

docs.title: What a crash leaves behind
docs.text:
The table is for a process kill (the page cache survives). A crash after a step leaves:

Crash after Visible generation Left on disk for the next open to remove 1 or 2 N a complete or partial new segment file 3 N new segment files and the new tombstone file 4 or 5 N and a temporary manifest 6 or 7 N+1 the files of generation N 8 N+1 whatever the cleanup had not yet deleted

TierTombstoneTest does the steps of the table with deleted, replaced and re-added ids in both generations. ManifestCrashTest and TierReopenTest run the publish with a hook that throws after each step and check which generation readLatest and open find, that the segments serve the same results as the in-memory graphs, and that the next open leaves exactly the files of that generation. TierHaltTest does the same with a real process: a child JVM halts itself (Runtime.halt, so no shutdown hook and no cleanup) at each step of a publish, and the parent opens the directory and compares its answers with those of the child's in-memory index. TierHaltLongTest (slow) does that for every step in each of three checkpoints with eight seeds, and TierKillLongTest (slow) kills a child that publishes in a loop at random moments (SIGKILL on Linux), opens the directory after each kill, and goes on in the same directory with the next child. The slow tests run on JDK 21 and 25. TierPowerCutTest starts from the files at each step and takes away what the publish order does not yet make durable at that step (a name that was not flushed, the bytes of the temporary manifest), and it also breaks the order on purpose (the rename reached the disk and the bytes of the manifest, of the new segment or of the tombstone file did not). In every case open serves exactly generation N or exactly generation N+1 and leaves exactly its files. None of those checks that the flushes are issued in the right order.

SimulatedFsCrashTest does, on a simulated file system. It records every write, flush, rename and delete of three publishes (the third after a merge, so it also deletes files), then builds the directories a crash can leave after each of those changes: a file keeps what was flushed and may keep all, part, none, or a torn mix of what was written later, and each new name, rename or delete since the last flush of its directory may or may not be there, in every combination. Each directory must open as exactly generation N or exactly generation N+1 (nothing before the first one is there), answer as the in-memory index of that generation did, hold only that generation's files afterwards, and take the next publish. The test also removes the flushes one at a time and expects a broken directory: every file flush is needed, so is the flush of the directory after the rename (step 7), and the flush of step 3 is needed for the first generation. In later generations a crash that loses a name because step 3 is missing still opens generation N, which is whole until step 7 has returned. A third run kills the process after each change, opens the directory in the next process, and crashes during and after that open. Two more publish into a directory that checkpoint makes itself, once straight through and once retried after a kill while the directory was made.

The claim stays a process kill. The simulated file system is a model: it shows that the library asks for its flushes in an order that holds under it, not what a particular file system or drive does when the power goes, and it does not run on Windows, where the directory cannot be flushed.

docs.title: Open
docs.text:
TieredIndex.open(dir, config):

  1. Manifest.readLatest: list the manifests, newest first. For each, check magic, version, CRC, that every named file exists with the recorded length and a valid header, footer and locator, and that the tombstone file matches. The first that passes is current. A candidate that fails is skipped; a segment whose first eight bytes are not the magic fails like one with a bad header CRC. If none passes it throws CorruptException; an empty directory throws NoSuchFileException; a manifest in a newer format throws UnsupportedException at once.
  2. Compare the fingerprint with the configuration (dimension, metric, M, efConstruction, SQ8). A difference throws MismatchException.
  3. Read every segment with every section checksummed, and compare it with its manifest entry.
  4. Delete the files that the manifest does not name (orphans of a crashed publish, older generations).
  5. Restore the version counter, the epoch and the floor map (for each id with a marked row, one more than the largest marked version, which hides exactly the marked rows), and start the tier with the segments and an empty tail.

Any failure throws. The overload open(dir, dim, metric, config, rebuildSource) catches it and builds the tier from the records with rebuildFrom; openFallbackCause() tells why. The directory is left as it was in that case. The next checkpoint replaces its contents, with one exception: when open failed with UnsupportedException, checkpoint into that directory throws the same exception and changes nothing, so that an older reader does not destroy files of a newer format. A host that wants to give those files up deletes the directory.

open(dir, dim, metric, config, recordSource) adds, after step 5, the epoch comparison (another epoch gives a cold index), the drop of ids above the host's recovered maximum (rebuilt segments and a new generation before it returns), the liveness check, and the replay of the host's live records above the high-water id: see ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md.

docs.title: What the first cut leaves out
docs.text:
• Memory mapping. A segment is read into the heap arrays of SealedGraph. The graph, the writer, the merge, and GraphIndex.fromSealed reach the vectors (section VEC) through one internal interface, SealedVectors, whose only implementation is a heap array, so a mapped reader can replace that one section (#27). The other sections are used as arrays.
  • Replay of the tail by the library itself. The host replays what the segments lack through RecordSource.
  • The tail. checkpoint refuses a tier with a non-empty tail (an IllegalStateException).
  • Soft-deleted rows inside a segment file: SegmentWriter refuses a graph that has them. The tier does not make such graphs; it records hidden rows in the tombstone file.
  • Lazy and chunked CRC verification. Every section is verified at open.
  • The fixed-stride layer 0 layout and padded rows.
  • Formats for the flat tail and for IVF.
  • A marker for an unclean shutdown.
  • A claim about power loss. The order of the flushes is tested on a simulated file system only.
  • Per-segment repair: any integrity failure rebuilds the whole tier.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

Experimental. The sources come from the first experiment and were imported unchanged except for the test wrappers and the small edits listed under "Import notes". Measurements of the experiment live in a private harness and are not published yet. The harness for new measurements of the tier is in the repository (BENCHMARKS.md). The result files committed so far are listed, with what they do not claim, in EVIDENCE.md: one study on generated data, one run per arm, which says nothing about speed.

docs.title: What exists
docs.text:
Each part has the test programs of the experiment, wrapped as JUnit 5 tests that CI runs on JDK 21 and 25 (see README). The fast tests also run on arm64: Linux with JDK 21 and 25, macOS with JDK 21 (none of these jobs is a required check). They also run on Windows x64 with JDK 21 (fast tests (Windows x64, JDK 21), a required check). The slow tests run on x86-64 Linux; on Windows x64 only the two slow crash tests run, TierHaltLongTest and TierKillLongTest (slow crash tests (Windows x64, JDK 21)).

Part What exists Tests Flat tier FlatIndex with NONE, SQ8, and BINARY scans, compaction, serialize and load, scalar twin kernels Correctness program, threaded program (5 s fast, 20 s and 60 s slow), correctness again with the scalar twins Kernels on the JVM With the Vector API, x86-64 vectorizes the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16. On aarch64 the fp32 kernels use VKernels and those other four use the 128-bit forms of NKernels (Kernels.JVM_NARROW), because VKernels has no fast form for 128-bit lanes (its int8 dot ran 138 times slower than scalar in CI). Hamming is scalar. A JVM with 128-bit lanes that is not aarch64 uses the scalar twins for those four. Not done: AVX-512 and SVE JvmQuantRoutingTest (the routing and the agreement with the scalar twins), KernDiffTest; the smoke mode jvm-vector on arm64 Linux checks the routing and fails when the int8 dot takes more than 10 times the scalar twin (#52) Graph tier GraphIndex (concurrent HNSW, delete, consolidate, optional SQ8), SealedGraph, seal and fromSealed in memory, SealedGraph.serialize and load (one segment file, CRC32C per section) Functional program (quick mode), threaded program with background consolidate (5 s fast, 60 s slow for fp32 and SQ8), latency during consolidate (slow), segment round trip and damage tests, the functional, threaded, and segment programs again with the scalar twins, a differential test of the vector and scalar graph kernels, and a test that builds and searches a tier in a JVM without the Vector API module IVF IvfIndex as a standalone index: lazy training, background retrain with atomic swap, drift detection, compaction Single-threaded program at n = 6000 (fast, vector and scalar) and n = 20000 (slow), drift program (slow), threaded program (5 s fast, 10 s slow) Tier TieredIndex: exact tail, sealed graph segments, merge, tombstones with a version floor, apply(batch) and awaitCapacity, rebuildFrom (also with an epoch and a snapshot position), checkpoint and open for a tier with an empty tail (segments, tombstones and a manifest per generation, format), and open with a record source (epoch check, durable prefix, liveness check, replay) The tier program, one test at a time (fast), the 10 s threaded test (slow), reopen, manifest and crash-step tests (fast), the record-id reuse tests (see below), the batch tests (see below) Native image Two image variants, built by the workflow, none a required check. The scalar image (job native image smoke, native image smoke (arm64 Linux) on arm64 Linux, and native image smoke (macOS arm64) on macOS arm64, GraalVM Community 21.0.2): the library and the program NativeSmoke (in src/smoke) are compiled, run once on a JVM without the Vector API module, built into a native image, and the image is run; the program checks that the scalar kernels are in use and that no jdk.incubator.vector class is present. The vector image (jobs native image smoke (vector, x86-64 Linux), (vector, arm64 Linux), and (vector, macOS arm64), plus native image smoke (vector, Windows x64), GraalVM Community 25.0.2, built with --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -H:+VectorAPISupport): in an image every kernel with a Vector API form (the fp32 dot and squared L2, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16) uses it through NKernels, with a species fixed at build time (256 bits on x86-64, 128 bits on aarch64), and hamming, which has no Vector API form, stays scalar; the program checks that Kernels.VECTOR and Kernels.NATIVE_VECTOR are true in the image, that NKernels was initialized at build time, the lanes, and that every kernel returns the bits of its NKernels method and agrees with its scalar twin. Results in an image can differ from the JVM by rounding. Both variants print informational SPEED lines, one per kernel. In both the program builds a flat index (three metrics in fp32, and SQ8 with each of its four kernels), an IVF index, a graph index, and a tier (fp32 and SQ8), and compares every answer with an exact scan after adds, background seals, a tail, deletes, sealNow, id reuse, mergeNow, and deletes after the merge NativeSmoke in the jobs; a failed check, a recall below the bar (0.9 for fp32, 0.8 for SQ8, 1.0 for the exact flat scan), or a failed image build fails the job

The wrappers assert two things per program: zero failed checks, and at least the number of checks the program reported in earlier runs of the experiment. The program code itself is not changed in a way that weakens an assertion.

docs.title: Record-id reuse and tombstones
docs.text:
A host database frees a record id and later gives it to a new record, so the tier sees delete(id) followed by add(id, newVector). The version floor of TieredIndex keeps the old copies of an id hidden while the new vector is visible. Tests cover this (#5). They use a model that holds the current vector of every id and keeps the older vectors, so a resurrected vector is recognised by its score.

Cases, each on a fresh index:

Case What it does a_tail The old copy sits in the active tail: delete 30 percent, re-add 80 percent of them with new vectors, delete and re-add again, then seal a2_tail_and_segments The old copies sit in one segment and in the tail: delete, re-add, seal, merge b_sealed The old copies sit in sealed segments: delete, re-add (the new vector in the tail, the old one below the floor), seal beside the old copies, delete and re-add again, seal, merge c1_reuse_in_merge Re-add, and delete then re-add, inside a running merge of the segments that hold the old copies; then again after the merge c2_delete_in_merge Delete, delete then re-add, delete then re-add then delete, replace, and brand-new ids, all inside a running merge; no delete may be lost when the merged segment is swapped in e_floor_chain One set of ids goes through four generations, each in its own segment, so the floor moves up four times; then a merge s_seal_window Operations inside the publish window of a seal, with the frozen tail holding every old copy (before the swap) and right after the swap, using setSealHooks f_fuzz_background Slow variant only: the background worker seals and merges while one writer reuses, replaces and deletes ids and one reader searches all the time; a hit counts only for an id that was untouched for the whole search

Every checkpoint searches plain, with the id alone allowed, and under Freshness.SEALED_ONLY, with the current vector and with an older vector of the id as the query. A deleted id, an older vector's score, a repeated id, a wrong score, or a reused id at rank 1 for its old vector fails the run. size() and stats().live() are compared with the model, and the floor map must be empty after a full merge in the deterministic cases. A merge window or seal window that is not reached fails the run, it is never skipped.

The tests are RidReuseTest (fast: n = 3000, dimension 32 and 128, two seeds, all deterministic cases, no reader thread), RidReuseLongTest and RidReuseBigLongTest (slow: all cases including the background case, with a concurrent reader that counts a hit only for an id untouched while the search ran; n = 3000 with three seeds on three configurations, and n = 20000), RidReuseSwapRaceTest (fast, about one second: a search paused inside its allow predicate while mergeNow() swaps and cleans up the floor), RebuildSwapRaceTest (fast: two searches paused inside their allow predicate while rebuildFrom swaps the rebuilt state in), and RidReuseMutantTest and RidReuseMutantLongTest. The probe itself is RidReuseProbe.

The probe found a race between a search and a merge swap (#26): a search that started before the swap could return an id that was deleted before it started, or an older vector of an id that was deleted and added again, because the merge removed the floor entries that the old segments still needed. The fix: a search counts itself on the view it reads, a view that a swap replaces while searches run on it is held, and the floor entries that a segment of a held view needs stay until those searches are done (the worker, awaitIdle, mergeNow, sealNow and checkpoint drop them then). The query path still takes no lock and starts no thread: it does one atomic add and one atomic subtract per search. RidReuseSwapRaceTest holds a search inside the first call of its filter, runs mergeNow(), lets the search go on, and checks the answer and that the entry is dropped afterwards; it failed on the code before the fix.

rebuildFrom had the same race on the recovery path (#28): it cleared the floor map before it swapped the rebuilt view in, so a search that was running on the old view could see a hidden copy as valid. It now swaps through the same publish call as a merge and settles the floor the same way, so the entries stay until the searches of the old view are done. RebuildSwapRaceTest holds one search with the vector of a deleted id and one with the older vector of an id that was added again, runs rebuildFrom with the live records, lets both go on, and checks the answers and that the floor map is empty after awaitIdle.

A probe that cannot fail is not a test, so the mutant tests check that it fails on a broken tier. The test reads TieredIndex.java, applies one single-line change (the anchor must occur exactly once), compiles the copy with the JDK compiler API into a temporary directory, and runs the probe in a class loader that prefers that directory. TieredIndex.java itself has no test hook. This needs a JDK, not a JRE: without a compiler the mutant tests are skipped with a message, and they fail when the CI environment variable is set.

Mutant Change The probe must report X0 none (control) a clean run M1 add removes the floor entry of the id instead of raising it staleHits above 0, in b_sealed M2 delete takes a version but writes no floor entry lostDeletes above 0, in b_sealed M3 cleanupFloor drops every entry after a merge a wrong answer in c2_delete_in_merge

docs.title: Id epoch and replay
docs.text:
The host names its numbering of ids with an epoch (#7, ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md). rebuildFrom(Supplier<Snapshot>, long) rebuilds from the host's snapshot without the write lock: the library records the writes that arrive during the build and applies them after the swap, adds at or below the snapshot position skipped. checkpoint stores the epoch and the high-water id (the largest id a segment holds) in the manifest, which already had the two fields, so the format version is the same. open(dir, dim, metric, config, RecordSource) discards persisted state of another epoch (a cold index), drops held ids above the id the host recovered and makes that durable before it returns, hides ids that the host no longer holds, and adds the host's live records above the high-water id to the tail.

The tests use FakeHost, a host that holds the records, mints increasing ids, and forgets its unflushed transactions in a simulated crash: EpochReplayTest (deterministic, fast), EpochReplayStressTest (a crash and reopen loop with random fault points, and a host thread that writes while the tier is rebuilt; three seeds, fast), and EpochReplayLongTest (the same, longer, slow). Not covered: power loss, a crash inside the replay itself, a crash inside the publish that open makes when it drops rows, a check of the id order, and a delete that the library persisted and the host then forgot (the host flushes its deletes before it lets the library checkpoint).

docs.title: Atomic batches
docs.text:
TieredIndex.apply(batch) applies the adds and then the deletes of one host transaction under one hold of the write lock, and a search sees all of the batch or none of it (#10). Applying the same batch again changes nothing visible. awaitCapacity(deadlineNanos) is the separate back pressure check: apply never waits for the worker and does not look at the hard tail limit, so one batch can take the tail above it.

The tail and the floor map change in place, so one volatile write of a new view cannot cover a batch. A batch counter does: it is odd while a batch is applied and even otherwise. A search waits while it is odd and reads it again after its scan, and when it changed, the scan is thrown away and run again. The query path still takes no lock and creates no thread: one volatile read before the scan, one fence and one read after it. A search that meets a batch waits for it (the length of one batch), and a stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search.

The tests are ApplyBatchTest (fast) and ApplyStressTest (slow). ApplyBatchTest checks that the whole batch is visible after apply returns, that a batch with a bad vector changes nothing, that applying a batch again changes nothing visible (also after a seal), that a search held inside its first allow call while a batch is applied answers from the state before the batch or the state after it and never from a mixture (once with the old id in the tail and once with the old id in a segment), that apply does not wait for a worker that is inside a seal, and the behavior of awaitCapacity at the hard tail limit. ApplyStressTest runs updater threads that move groups of ids from one generation to the next in batches while searcher threads check that a group always shows exactly its ids of one generation, on a tail and on a tier that seals and merges all the time.

docs.title: Deadline and cancellation
docs.text: The TieredIndex.search overloads that take a SearchContext stop when it says so and throw SearchCancelledException (#11). A context that returns true from partialWanted() finds in the exception the best hits of the tails and segments that were read to the end, and nothing when a batch was applied during the search (#134, PartialResultTest). Without that request the exception carries no hits. The context is polled at the start, before each tail and each segment, at least once every 1024 candidates inside them, and while a search waits for a batch. While it never expires, a search answers like one without a context. The standalone indexes (FlatIndex, GraphIndex, IvfIndex) take no context. The tests are in SearchContextTest (fast). The harness for the cost of polling is described in BENCHMARKS.md.

docs.title: Graph self-search recall
docs.text:
The graph index is approximate, so a search for a vector that is equal to an inserted one can miss it (#38). Measured at the default ef (100): at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors the graph index misses a query equal to an inserted vector at about 1.2e-4 to 4.0e-4 per probe (1,600,000 probes in each of four modes, 188 to 636 misses per mode). Every one of the 1,260 misses that were diagnosed was reachable from the entry point on layer 0, and a search at ef 1000 found 1,254 of them. At the size of the threaded program (below 67,000 vectors) there was 1 miss in 112 runs of 3,360 probes. These are measurements of the default ef, not a guarantee, and the rate rises with the size of the index.

The threaded program (GraphConcurrencyTest) therefore checks read-your-writes in two parts. Exact membership: right after add returned, the id must be in the index, with no tolerance. It is read through the id-to-ordinal map and the node state (GraphIndex.containsForTest, a package-private accessor for tests), not through a search. Self-search: a recall check that searches for the vector just inserted at ten times the default ef (1000) and fails on more than 1 miss per run (3,360 probes in the 60 s program). Each run prints one line, RYW membership checks=N missing=0 selfSearchMisses=K of M. GraphReadYourWritesTest (fast) covers both parts on 3,000 vectors with a tolerance of 0, and checks that the probe reports an id that is not in the index.

docs.title: What does not exist yet
docs.text:
• Serialization of IVF and of the flat tail. FlatIndex has its own serialize and load. The graph segments and a tier with an empty tail have the first cut (SEGMENT-FORMAT.md): copy-based reads, no memory mapping, no persisted tail (checkpoint refuses a tier with a tail), every section verified at open. When open fails, the host falls back to rebuildFrom.
  • Engine integration. Nothing here is wired into ArcadeDB or any other engine.
  • IVF as a segment type of the tier. IvfIndex is standalone.
  • Native-image coverage beyond the smoke job. The program does not write or read segment files (checkpoint, open), does not call rebuildFrom, and uses no concurrent writers; the image is built on Linux (x86-64 and arm64) and on macOS arm64 in CI, and on Windows x64 in the vector job only (there is no scalar image job on Windows), and it is not published.
  • A stable API. 0.1.0 is the first release. Until 1.0 a breaking change to the supported surface needs a new minor version (API.md). The version rule, the steps and the Maven Central details are in RELEASING.md.
  • Published measurements. The experiment's own measurements are in a private harness. The harness Bench (BENCHMARKS.md) is in the repository and the CI job bench smoke runs it at 10,000 vectors. The only committed result files are recall results on generated data (EVIDENCE.md).
  • The longer mode of the graph test program (a recall curve at n = 20000) is not wired into the JUnit tests.

docs.title: Import notes
docs.text:
• The Java package is ai.humem.tiervec, the name of the library. It was renamed from the package of the first import before the first release, so it is not a breaking change. The system property that forces the scalar twins is ai.humem.tiervec.scalar.
  • Comments and Javadoc in the sources were rewritten in plain words: the experiment-internal names (requirement ids, fix numbers, rule names) are gone, and no code changed in that edit.
  • The graph test helper T was renamed GraphT, because the flat tests have their own T and both now live in one module and one package.
  • The test helpers got an exitOnFailure flag (default true, so a program run alone still ends the JVM on failure), and the end of each program's main is guarded by it. A JUnit wrapper sets it to false and reads the counters instead, because a System.exit would end the surefire JVM.
  • The micro-benchmark FlatMicro and the benchmark harness of the experiment are not part of this repository. Bench and NativeSmoke are new programs written for it, not imports.
  • One edit to a main source, GraphIndex.java (issue #3, found by the slow CI job): consolidate(), repairOrphans and seal() size their bitsets and arrays from a snapshot of nextOrd, and a concurrent add can publish a node allocated after the snapshot as the entry point (or, in repairOrphans, return one from its search), so the node index fell past the end. bit now reads an index past the end as not set, repairOrphans sizes its arrays to cover the entry point, and seal() ignores an entry point from after its snapshot. GraphConsolidateRaceTest builds that view without threads. It was pushed alone first and failed the fast job on the unfixed code.

docs.title: tiervec
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

A tiered vector index for agent-memory databases on the JVM.

Status: experimental. The API is not stable, the first release is 0.1.0, and nothing is wired into a database engine yet. No benchmark numbers are published. What is proven says what the repository shows today, and docs/STATUS.md has the detail.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
A library of vector-index algorithms meant to live inside a database engine, in the same process, with no network between the engine and the index. The first host is ArcadeDB.

The design follows the workload of an agent's memory: many small and medium collections, a steady stream of small writes, deletes and updates, and queries that must see a write right away.

  • Exact tail. Recent writes sit in a bounded buffer that is scanned exactly, so a write is visible to the next query without waiting for an index build.
  • Sealed segments. Older vectors live in immutable HNSW graph segments. Below a size threshold no graph is built and every search is an exact scan. Segments are merged in the background and swapped in atomically.
  • Tombstones with a version floor handle deletes and updates, including ids that a database reuses after a delete.
  • Scalar twins of every kernel (flat, IVF, and graph), chosen once per JVM, so every index, the graph tier and the tiered index included, also runs without the Vector API module.
  • Pure Java, no native dependencies. It also builds into a GraalVM native image, where every kernel except hamming (fp32, int8, SQ8, and block) uses the Vector API too (see Native image).

The repository also holds a standalone IVF (inverted file) index, which is not a tier segment yet. The host engine would own persistence, transactions and recovery: the tier can rebuild all of its derived state from the raw vectors. Serialization exists for the flat index and, as a first cut, for a settled tier: segment files with a manifest, written by TieredIndex.checkpoint and read by TieredIndex.open (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md). docs/DESIGN.md describes what the code does.

docs.title: What is proven
docs.text:
Every row says what the repository itself shows, and links the evidence. "Not measured yet" means no number is published here.

Question Where it stands Evidence Does it build and pass its tests? Yes, on Linux x86-64 (JDK 21 and 25, fast and slow tests), Linux arm64, macOS arm64 and Windows x64 (fast tests on these three, and on Windows the two slow crash tests too). Native image smoke jobs run on the same four platforms. Platform support, docs/STATUS.md Sizes the tests use The tests run on small collections. The long id-reuse test (RidReuseBigLongTest) and the long IVF program use 20,000 vectors, and the threaded graph program stays below 67,000. A self-search probe on the graph index ran at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors. docs/STATUS.md Speed and recall at scale Barely measured, and nothing here is proven at 1,000,000 vectors or at 10,000,000. The only committed result files are from one study on generated data at 100,000 and 1,000,000 vectors, one run per arm on a laptop's low-power cores, so they say nothing about speed or about real embeddings. A harness for these measurements exists, and CI runs it at 10,000 vectors as a smoke test. docs/EVIDENCE.md, docs/BENCHMARKS.md, docs/STATUS.md Concurrent readers and writers Tested at small sizes: threaded programs of 5 to 60 seconds, batch stress tests, and tests that hold a search inside a merge or a seal. Concurrent writers at scale: not proven. docs/STATUS.md Deletes, updates, reused ids, atomic batches Tested, including races between a search and a merge or a rebuild. The races found so far (#3, #26, #28) have tests. docs/STATUS.md, docs/STATUS.md Restart and recovery A tier with an empty tail can be checkpointed and reopened, deleted and replaced ids included. Tests stop the publish after each step (a simulated process kill, and a child JVM that halts itself at each step), flip bits in every byte that a CRC covers, forge files with valid CRCs, and open the directories that a power cut could leave if the flushes keep the documented order. The order itself is tested on a simulated file system that drops what was not flushed; that is a model, so power loss is not claimed. docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md, docs/STATUS.md Native image Smoke tests build and run an image and compare every answer with an exact scan. They do not cover segment files, rebuildFrom or concurrent writers. The image is not published. docs/STATUS.md Inside a database engine No. Nothing here is wired into ArcadeDB or any other engine. docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md Release 0.1.0 is the first release. The Maven coordinates are ai.humem:tiervec. The API is not stable. CHANGELOG.md, docs/RELEASING.md

Known limits

  • Graph search is approximate. At the default ef (100), a query equal to an inserted vector is missed at about 1.2e-4 to 4.0e-4 per probe at 100,000 to 200,000 vectors, and the rate rises with the size of the index. A search at ef 1000 found 1,254 of the 1,260 misses that were diagnosed. The hardware of this measurement is not recorded. (details)
  • A filtered search with a small allowed share (about 0.01) spends most of its cost on a walk that falls back to an exact scan. The opt-in filterScanBelow skips the walk, it is off by default, a filter that says how many ids it allows (SizedIdFilter) is scanned exactly when it allows at most ef, and the range of shares where a scan pays is not measured yet (#12, docs/DESIGN.md).
  • checkpoint needs an empty tail (sealNow): the tail is not persisted. Reads copy the file into memory, with no memory mapping (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md).
  • A search that meets a batch waits for it, and a stream of batches that follow each other faster than one scan takes can starve a search (docs/STATUS.md).
  • In a native image a result can differ from the JVM by rounding. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
mvn -B -ntp verify            # fast tests: Vector API kernels, then the scalar twins
mvn -B -ntp verify -Pslow     # the long concurrency and stress tests (tag "slow")

The tests are test programs, wrapped as JUnit 5 tests. A wrapper runs the program, asserts that no check failed, and asserts that at least the expected number of checks ran. The benchmark harness is not part of the Maven build: docs/BENCHMARKS.md says how to compile and run it.

docs.title: Native image
docs.text:
The library runs in a GraalVM native image. The CI job native image smoke builds the scalar image, and the jobs native image smoke (vector, ...) build the vector image on x86-64 and arm64 Linux and on macOS arm64 (GraalVM Community 25.0.2). The scalar image also builds on arm64 Linux (native image smoke (arm64 Linux)) and on macOS arm64 (native image smoke (macOS arm64)). The job native image smoke (vector, Windows x64) builds the vector image on Windows x64; there is no scalar image job on Windows.

  • In an image every kernel that has a Vector API form uses it through NKernels (flat, IVF, and graph): the fp32 dot and l2sq, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16. The species is fixed when the image is built: 256 bits on x86-64, 128 bits on aarch64 (where the Vector API has no 32-bit byte species, so the byte kernels load 64 or 128 bits of bytes and split them into parts). The Vector API kernels of the JVM are more than 10 times slower than scalar code in an image, so the image does not use them; NKernels is the form that the image compiles to SIMD code.
  • hamming has no Vector API form and stays scalar, in an image and on a JVM. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (the species stay 256 and 128 bits until measured).
  • A result in an image can differ from a result on a JVM by rounding, because the lane sum of NKernels has the order of the instruction. Results are still bitwise equal between two calls on equal data within one image.
  • To build an image with the Vector API kernels, give the image builder --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector -H:+VectorAPISupport. The jar carries META-INF/native-image/ai.humem/tiervec/native-image.properties, which sets --initialize-at-build-time=ai.humem.tiervec.NKernels for an application that has the jar on its class path; the species must be fixed at build time, or the kernels are slow. -H:+VectorAPISupport is an experimental option of GraalVM 25, and it needs GraalVM 25 or newer.
  • Without --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector the image has the scalar twins for every kernel. -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true forces the scalar twins in an image as well, when the property is set before the library is first used (an image takes -D options on its command line).
  • The smoke program prints informational SPEED lines, one per kernel (dot, dotI8, dotF8, dotF8x4, and block16 per block of 16 vectors), with the median time of 1,000,000 calls on 768 dimensions next to the scalar twin. They are not a bar.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• JDK 21 or newer. CI builds and tests with Temurin 21 and 25 on x86-64 Linux, and runs the fast tests on arm64 Linux (JDK 21 and 25) and arm64 macOS (JDK 21). The job fast tests (Windows x64, JDK 21) runs the fast tests on Windows x64, and slow crash tests (Windows x64, JDK 21) the two slow crash tests. What a checkpoint guarantees differs on Windows: see the table in SEGMENT-FORMAT.md.
  • Maven 3.9 or newer.
  • The Vector API is an incubator module in these JDKs. Compile with --add-modules jdk.incubator.vector, and run with it to get the Vector API kernels; the pom.xml sets it for the compiler and for the test JVMs. At run time the module is optional: every kernel (flat, IVF, and graph) falls back to its scalar twin when the module is missing, or when -Dai.humem.tiervec.scalar=true is set.
  • On a JVM with the Vector API, x86-64 vectorizes the fp32 dot and l2sq, the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16. On aarch64 (NEON, 128-bit float lanes) the fp32 dot and l2sq use the JVM kernels and the int8 dot, the SQ8 dots, and block16 use the 128-bit forms of NKernels. hamming is scalar everywhere. A JVM with 128-bit lanes that is not aarch64 runs those four as scalar code. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).
  • Nothing else at run time. JUnit 5 is a test dependency.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
There are three tiers. For tier 1, each row names the CI job that proves it. A job marked "required" must pass before a pull request can merge into main. The other jobs do not block it. The arm64 fast tests, the native image jobs and the slow tests do not run on an ordinary pull request: they run on main after the merge, and the slow tests also once a day and on a pull request that carries the label ci:slow (CONTRIBUTING.md). All jobs run on GitHub-hosted runners.

Tier 1: tested in CI on every change

The full slow tests run on Linux x86-64 only; Windows x64 runs the two slow crash tests. There is no scalar-kernel native image job on Windows. The native image jobs run on a push to main that changes src/main, src/smoke or their workflow file. On a pull request they run only when it changes src/smoke, META-INF/native-image, Kern.java, Kernels.java, NKernels.java or their workflow file.

Tier 2: measured. None yet. The result files committed so far (docs/EVIDENCE.md) are recall results of one run per arm on a laptop's low-power cores, and they move no platform into this tier. The harness is described in docs/BENCHMARKS.md; a row moves here when a result file with its hardware, JDK and commit is committed under results/. The SPEED lines that the native image jobs print are informational, and the one measurement in the repository (the graph self-search recall in docs/STATUS.md) does not record its hardware. The shared GitHub runners are not a benchmark machine: a timing from them is a ratio between two things measured in the same run, not an absolute speed. A row moves here when its numbers and its hardware are published.

Tier 3: best effort. The code is plain Java 21 and has no native dependency, so it is expected to work, but nothing checks it and a problem there is fixed when it is cheap to do.

  • macOS on Intel (x86-64): no CI job.
  • Other JDK vendors and other JDK versions than 21 and 25: only Temurin 21 and 25 are tested.
  • Other Linux distributions and other CPU features: the CI runners fix them. AVX-512 and SVE are not used (#52).

Out: Windows on ARM, until GraalVM and the libraries around it support it. Nothing here builds or tests it.

All notable changes to tiervec are in this file. The layout follows Keep a Changelog. The version rule and the steps of a release are in docs/RELEASING.md. Until 1.0, a breaking change to the supported surface (docs/API.md) needs a new minor version.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• A partial result of a stopped search, on request: a SearchContext that returns true from the new default method partialWanted() finds in SearchCancelledException.partialHits() the best hits of the tails and segments that were read to the end, and nothing when a batch was applied during the search. Without the request nothing changes (issue #134).
  • SizedIdFilter: a LongPredicate that says how many ids it allows. When the count is at most ef, TieredIndex, GraphIndex and SealedGraph scan the allowed ids exactly instead of walking the graph; a wrong count never changes which ids may be returned. Also liveCount() and Capability.SELECTIVE_PLAN. The threshold is not measured (issue #12).
  • HostEnv: a tier that runs on the host's executor, creates no thread of its own, asks a permit before every seal, merge and rebuild, and reads a memory budget; the peak estimate is not measured (issue #13).
  • The configuration as text: Config.toMap, Config.fromMap (refuses an unknown key, for the creation of an index), Config.fromStoredMap (reports and ignores one, so a downgrade opens), and Config.fingerprint over the data-affecting settings. TieredIndex.reconfigure changes the search-time knobs graph.efSearch and splitBeam of an open index (issue #18).
  • TieredIndex.contractVersion and capabilities (ContractVersion, Capability), metrics and bindMetrics (MetricSink), health (TieredIndex.Health), and the exception base TiervecException with CorruptStateException, ClosedException, and BuildRefusedException; SearchCancelledException extends the base now (issue #18).
  • TieredIndex.MergeMode and Config.withMergeMode: with INSERT, a merge that takes the largest segment copies its graph and inserts the vectors of the other inputs instead of rebuilding everything. The default stays REBUILD, and the cost of the two has not been measured. Config has one more record component, and the constructors without it still exist (issue #16).
  • SearchContext and SearchCancelledException: the TieredIndex.search overloads that take a context stop at a deadline or a cancel flag of the host. The context is polled at least once every 1024 candidates, and a stopped search returns no partial result (issue #11). A call that passes a literal null as the fourth argument of search needs a cast now, because two overloads accept it.
  • Benchmark harness: --data reads a real embedding set that scripts/prep_real_dataset.py converts from parquet (raw float32 files with exact answers), and --engine jvector builds and searches the same data with JVector at the same M and efConstruction, in the bench profile only (JVector is not a dependency of the library). A CI smoke runs both on a small generated set (docs/BENCHMARKS.md, issue #108).
  • Benchmark harness: --quant int8 runs JVector on int8 vectors, with and without a float32 rerank, and --quant sq8 builds the tier with SQ8 codes. --targets reports latency at matched recall, --disk the size of the written index, --props checks that a write is found by the next search and that a reused id never answers with its old vector, and --shares now works with the JVector arm. The bench profile moves to JVector 4.1.0-rc.1 (issue #118).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: TieredIndex.open(dir, config) throws the unchecked CorruptStateException for damaged files, where it threw the checked SegmentFormat.CorruptException. Catch CorruptStateException; its cause is the old exception. UnsupportedException, MismatchException, NoSuchFileException, and the open overloads with a rebuild source behave as before (issue #18).
  • Breaking: after close, the calls that read or change vectors or files (add, delete, apply, search, rebuildFrom, sealNow, mergeNow, checkpoint) throw ClosedException. Before, most of them still worked on the memory of the closed index. A build that close interrupts throws it too, where it threw IllegalStateException (issue #18).
  • One process owns an index directory, and the library now enforces it: checkpoint and open lock the file LOCK in the directory, keep the lock until close, and throw the new DirectoryLockedException when another process holds it. The open overloads with a rebuild source throw it too and do not rebuild (issue #27).
  • checkpoint accepts a tier with deleted, replaced and re-added ids. It writes the hidden rows into the tombstone file, and open rebuilds the floor map from them. Before, it threw IllegalStateException until a merge had rewritten every segment with a hidden row. Version 0.1.x refuses a directory with a hidden row (UnsupportedException) and does not overwrite it. RecordSource.isLive is not called for an id whose copies were all hidden at the checkpoint (issue #27).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• sealNow, mergeNow, rebuildFrom and checkpoint get their turn while writes go on. Before, the background worker could take the lock of the builds again right after each task, so under steady writes such a call could wait for as long as the writes went on (#144).
  • The fp32 graph kernels of a JVM (VKern) sum the lanes in a fixed order, like the flat kernels. Before, the sum was reduceLanes(ADD), whose order depends on the JIT tier, so the same search could return a score one ulp apart before and after compilation. This showed as a rare failure of SegmentForgedFileTest on arm64 (#104). A score can differ from the one of 0.1.0 in the last bit.
  • A flipped bit in the major version of a segment header is damage (CorruptException, section HEADER), so TieredIndex.open falls back to the previous generation. Before, the version was read before the header CRC, and one flipped bit there in the newest segment made the whole open fail with UnsupportedException. A larger major version with an intact header is still refused (#116).
  • A flipped bit in the major version of a manifest is damage (CorruptException), so TieredIndex.open falls back to the previous generation and a later checkpoint replaces the files. Before, the version was read before the CRC: open and every checkpoint into the directory failed with UnsupportedException (#123).
  • A segment file whose first eight bytes are damaged is refused with CorruptException (section HEADER) and not UnsupportedException, and the message names the file and the field. Before, one flipped bit in the magic of the newest segment made TieredIndex.open fail, where a flipped bit in the header, footer or locator made it fall back to the previous generation. A larger major version is still an UnsupportedException that is refused, not skipped (#83).
  • TieredIndex.open flushes the directory before it deletes the files of an older generation. Before, after a process was killed between the rename of a manifest and the flush that follows it, the next open removed the previous generation while the rename was still unflushed, so a power cut at that point could leave no generation at all (#125).
  • checkpoint flushes the name of a directory that it creates into its parent. Before, a power cut after the first checkpoint into a new directory had returned could lose the whole directory (#126).
The library code is unchanged from 0.1.0: no source file changed. The changes are in the release workflow and the pom.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Creating the GitHub release now publishes to Maven Central by itself and verifies the result (checksums, signatures, the built jars, a resolution from a fresh local repository), so the Publish click in the Central Portal is gone (docs/RELEASING.md).

The first release. It is the sources of the first experiment, imported and brought to the supported surface in docs/API.md. Nothing was released under the old package name. Details are in docs/STATUS.md.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• FlatIndex: exact scan with optional SQ8 or binary codes, compaction, serialize and load.
  • GraphIndex: a concurrent HNSW graph with delete, consolidate, and optional SQ8.
  • IvfIndex: a standalone inverted-file index with lazy training, background retrain and drift detection.
  • TieredIndex: an exact tail, sealed graph segments, background merges, tombstones with a version floor, atomic batches (apply, awaitCapacity), rebuildFrom, and an opt-in scan-first plan for filtered searches (filterScanBelow).
  • Persistence of a settled tier: TieredIndex.checkpoint and TieredIndex.open, with segment files and a manifest (docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md), and RecordSource for reconciling a reopened tier with the records of a host database (docs/ID-EPOCH-AND-REPLAY.md).
  • Scalar twins of every kernel, used when the Vector API module is missing, and Vector API kernels for aarch64 and for GraalVM native images.
  • A GraalVM native image smoke test on Linux (x86-64 and arm64), macOS arm64 and Windows x64.
  • CI on JDK 21 and 25, with the fast tests also on arm64 and on Windows x64.
  • Community files (CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY, SUPPORT, and the issue and pull request templates) and the platform support table in the README.
  • The supported public surface and the stability policy (docs/API.md).
  • A benchmark harness for the tier (src/bench, docs/BENCHMARKS.md) with a CI smoke at 10,000 vectors. No result file is published yet.
  • Maven Central publishing for ai.humem:tiervec: the metadata Central requires in pom.xml, a release profile (sources jar, javadoc jar, GnuPG signatures, upload to the Central Portal), and the workflow release-central.yml with a dry run (docs/RELEASING.md).
  • The documentation is published as a release version with the alias latest when a version tag is pushed, and dev stays the label of main.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Package renamed from com.humemai.vec to ai.humem.tiervec (no other change). The system property that forces the scalar twins was renamed with it, from humemai.vec.scalar to ai.humem.tiervec.scalar.

docs.title: Contributing to tiervec
docs.text:
Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

tiervec is a Java library of vector-index algorithms that is meant to run inside a database engine. It is experimental: the first release is 0.1.0 and the API is not stable yet (see docs/STATUS.md). Small, focused contributions are welcome.

docs.title: Licence
docs.text:
tiervec is licensed under the Apache License 2.0. When you submit a contribution, you agree that it is licensed under the same terms (Section 5 of the licence). You keep your copyright. There is no separate contributor agreement.

Do not copy code or text into the repository unless its licence is compatible with Apache 2.0. Papers and libraries that the work builds on are listed in THIRD_PARTY.md. The library has no run-time dependencies, and a new one needs a strong reason.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• A security problem is not an issue. Follow SECURITY.md.
  • A question is not a bug. See SUPPORT.md.
  • Search the open issues first. If your idea is not there, open an issue and say what problem it solves. For a new feature or a change in behavior, wait for an answer before you write much code.
  • Read docs/DESIGN.md and docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md. They say what the library does and what it promises to a host database.

docs.title: Build and test
docs.text:
You need JDK 21 or newer and Maven 3.9 or newer.

mvn -B -ntp verify            # fast tests: Vector API kernels, then the scalar twins
mvn -B -ntp verify -Pslow     # the long concurrency and stress tests (tag "slow")

The fast tests run on every pull request, on JDK 21 and 25. The slow tests take about 40 minutes per JDK, so they do not run on an ordinary pull request: see What CI runs, and when. You do not have to run them on your own machine.

docs.title: Build the documentation
docs.text:
The site at https://docs.humem.ai/tiervec/dev/ is built with MkDocs Material from the README, the other Markdown files in the repository root, and docs/. The hook docs-site/hooks.py turns the root files into pages and rewrites relative links: a link to another page stays a link to that page, and a link to any other file in the repository becomes a link to it on GitHub. The design system in docs/brand is a vendored copy. Do not edit it: change it in humemai/design-system and vendor it again. bash docs/brand/verify.sh checks the copy. To build the site as the check does:

uv run --no-project --python 3.12 --with-requirements docs-site/requirements.txt mkdocs build --strict

The build fails on a link that points nowhere. The workflow deploy-docs.yml publishes the site as dev when a change to the docs reaches main.

docs.title: Make a change
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository and branch from main.
  2. Keep the change small. One pull request does one thing.
  3. Add a test. A test for a bug fix must fail on the old code and pass on the new. Say in the pull request how you checked that.
  4. Run the fast tests. A change in a kernel must keep the scalar twin and the Vector API form in agreement (see KernDiffTest).
  5. Update the documentation that your change makes wrong: the README, the files in docs/, and the Javadoc.
  6. Open a pull request. Say what changed and why, and write Closes #N for the issue it fixes.

Commit messages start with the area, then a short summary and the issue number, for example Tests: replace absolute throughput floors in concurrency tests with an overlap proof (#59).

Pull requests are squash-merged into main, so the history is linear.

docs.title: Checks that must pass
docs.text:
Five checks are required before a merge:

  • fast tests (JDK 21)
  • fast tests (JDK 25)
  • fast tests (Windows x64, JDK 21)
  • Ensure SHA pinned actions
  • docs build (strict)

The other jobs (the benchmark smoke, and the arm64 and native image jobs where they run) are not required. A failure there is read like any other failure.

docs.title: What CI runs, and when
docs.text:
When What runs Every pull request The fast tests (x86-64 Linux on JDK 21 and 25, Windows x64), the benchmark smoke, the documentation build and the workflow check. The Maven Central dry run starts only when the files it covers change. It ends in about 12 minutes. A pull request that changes src/smoke, META-INF/native-image, Kern.java, Kernels.java, NKernels.java or native-image.yml The same, and the native image jobs. A pull request from a release/ branch The same, and the fast tests on arm64 Linux and arm64 macOS. A pull request with the label ci:slow The same, the slow tests on JDK 21 and 25 (about 40 minutes each), and the two slow crash tests on Windows x64. Every push to main The jobs of every pull request, the arm64 fast tests and the slow tests. The native image jobs run when the push changes src/main, src/smoke or their workflow file. Every day at 19:17 UTC The slow tests, on the head of main.

To ask for the slow tests on a pull request, add the label ci:slow. If you cannot set labels, ask for it in the pull request and the maintainer adds it. The slow tests start when the label is added and run again on every later push to that pull request. Ask for them when a change touches what they cover: concurrent readers and writers, seals and merges, record-id reuse, or the batch paths. On a pull request without the label, the slow tests show as one skipped check, which is not a failure.

The slow tests also run by hand on any branch: gh workflow run slow-tests.yml --ref <branch>.

The arm64 fast tests and the native image jobs do not run on an ordinary pull request. When a change can behave differently on arm64 or in a native image (a kernel, for example), start them on the branch before the merge: gh workflow run ci.yml --ref <branch> (every job of ci.yml) and gh workflow run native-image.yml --ref <branch>. This needs write access, so ask the maintainer if you do not have it. When one of these jobs is red on main, the workflow opens the issue "arm64 tests are red on main" or "Native image jobs are red on main", or comments on it when it is already open.

When a slow run on main is red, the workflow opens the issue "Slow tests are red on main", or comments on it when it is already open. The slow tests are in .github/workflows/slow-tests.yml; the other tests are in ci.yml.

docs.title: Workflow files
docs.text: Every action in .github/workflows/ is pinned to a full commit SHA, with the version as a comment. A floating tag fails the check Ensure SHA pinned actions.

docs.title: Measurements
docs.text: Do not put a performance number in a pull request or in the documentation unless you can say how it was measured: the hardware, the JDK, the data, the number of runs. Timing numbers from the shared GitHub runners are useful as ratios between two things measured in the same run. They are not absolute speed.

docs.title: Conduct
docs.text: Be polite and be specific. Disagree with the code or the idea, not with the person. Harassment is not tolerated, and the maintainer may remove comments and block people who harass others.

docs.title: Security policy
docs.text: Experimental. The API is not stable and nothing here is wired into a database engine yet. What may change.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
Do not open a public issue for a security problem.

Use GitHub's private reporting: open the Security tab of the repository and choose Report a vulnerability. Or send an email to info@humem.ai with the subject tiervec security. Either way a maintainer reads it, replies, and works with you on a fix before anything is made public.

Please include:

  • The version or the commit of tiervec.
  • The JDK (the output of java -version), the operating system and the CPU architecture.
  • Whether the Vector API module is on (--add-modules jdk.incubator.vector), or the scalar twins are in use, or the code runs in a native image.
  • A description of the problem and its impact.
  • Steps to reproduce it, or a small program that shows it.

docs.title: What counts
docs.text:
tiervec is a library that runs in the process of its host. It opens no socket and reads no file that the host did not point it to. These are in scope:

  • A file in a segment directory that makes TieredIndex.open or SegmentReader read or write memory outside the file, loop without end, or allocate without a bound, other than by throwing an exception. The format checks its sections with CRC32C, but a CRC detects accidental damage and is no protection against tampering (see docs/SEGMENT-FORMAT.md), so a hostile file must still not do harm.
  • A search that returns a vector for an id that was deleted, or that returns data from another index.
  • A flaw in the build or in the workflow files that lets an outside party run code in CI or change a release.

A wrong answer, a crash on bad input that ends in an exception, and a slow query are ordinary bugs. Open an issue for them.

docs.title: Supported versions
docs.text: The first release is 0.1.0. A fix goes to the latest minor version as a new patch version, and main gets it too (see the version rule in docs/RELEASING.md).

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text: tiervec is a small open source project with one maintainer and no fixed response time. You get a reply, and credit in the fix if you want it. No bounty is paid.

docs.text:

tiervec is an open source library, maintained by HumemAI under the Apache License 2.0. It is experimental: the first release is 0.1.0, and the API can change (see docs/STATUS.md).

docs.title: Who maintains it
docs.text: The maintainer is @tae898. Every issue and pull request is assigned to the maintainer when it is opened.

docs.title: How to get help
docs.text: You want to Do this Report a bug Open an issue with the bug template. It asks for the JDK, the platform, and whether the Vector API is on. Ask how something works Read README.md, docs/DESIGN.md and docs/PROVIDER-CONTRACT.md. If they do not answer it, open an issue with the question label. Propose a feature Open an issue with the feature template. Report a security problem Follow SECURITY.md. Do not use a public issue.

docs.title: What to expect
docs.text:
This is best-effort support from one maintainer. There is no response-time promise, no commercial support, and no hosted service. Bugs that come with a short, runnable reproduction are fixed first.

Only the code on main is supported. A host that wants to depend on tiervec today should expect the API to change between versions (see docs/ROADMAP.md).
